The fog of war clears around Embervale, revealing a survival crafting masterpiece.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

What is it? A high-fantasy survival crafting RPG set in the genre's most impressive sandbox. Release date: October 15, 2026 (1.0) Expect to pay: $40/£35 Developer: Keen Games Publisher: Keen Games Reviewed on: RTX 4080, AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, 64GB RAM Steam Deck: Verified Link: Steam | Official site

High up on a mountain in the Albaneve Summits, just on the southern border of Enshrouded's new zone, I spot the perfect place for my next medieval building project. It seems safe with no nearby enemy spawns on the flat stretch of land, and there's even a cute frozen pond that gives it real Christmas-card appeal. I love it, and I'll love it even more once I've built a cliffside castle.

The only problem is I can't find a way up by climbing or gliding, so I'll have to make my own. I could build something, but that takes time, and I'm impatient. Instead, I behave like an absolute heathen—I bomb and pickaxe the hell out of the mountainside, carving a tunnel from the base to the top. It doesn't look great, but that's a problem for tomorrow's Flameborn.

That's always been one of my favorite parts of Enshrouded: you can destroy or build practically anything, anywhere in Embervale's voxel-based world. It's a survival crafting sandbox filled to the brim with handcrafted details, and every location still hidden by the fog of war could hold a new material, powerful weapon, or scenic vista. There's nothing quite like it, and just like the updates before, Enshrouded's 1.0 build keeps finding new, inventive ways to impress me long after I thought its well of surprises had run dry.

Enshrouded is a weird one. Not quite a traditional survival crafting game, but not a typical action RPG either. Its combat system and base building options are far more robust than most of its survival crafting cousins, but it's not nearly as brutal. I'm driven less by desperation and more by a desire to explore Embervale—a land devastated by a mysterious, malignant miasma known as (you guessed it) the Shroud. There's hardly a soul left in the world, so you learn more about its history from journals. Some are hastily scribbled by would-be heroes like you, while others are tragic retellings of someone's final days.

A few survivors remain as recruitable NPCs for your base. I love how lively they make player-made homes feel, even if the AI is a bit dopey.

One of my favorite additions in 1.0 is the voiceover added to every journal. The same narrator reads them all, giving the whole thing an endearing storybook feel as he shifts tone and pitch for different authors.

I found my favorite journal in a tiny, mountainside cave left by an old man grieving his wife. You can wander around the surrounding area for more environmental storytelling, but I have to warn you: some details got me teary-eyed.

So, for what must be the millionth time in my career, I stumble out of a mystical, sleepy haze confused and poorly dressed for the world I've awakened to. I am the Flameborn—a sort of ordained-by-god chosen one and the last hope for restoring the ruins of Embervale—but for now, I certainly don't feel that way. I just feel like some guy. It's a title I'll have to grow into, but will have to wait until I've upgraded from the aptly named 'ragged armor set'. Yeesh.

Enshrouded follows most of those rags-to-riches genre basics, so of course I'll graduate from an era of fighting with sticks and eating fistfuls of berries to magic-infused swords and Michelin-star meals. I've played so many of these games that the flow comes naturally now, but what I like most about Enshrouded's take on classic survival systems is that it drops the more punitive elements like fatigue, crafting chance, and even structural integrity.

Enshrouded has a robust set of custom difficulty options, but I learned the hard way to leave them alone until after you've tried the first dungeon.

An early access update added a custom setting for dehydration and starvation, but I much prefer playing without it .

There's cooking, farming, and even animal husbandry. Those systems are compelling enough as is, and don't gain anything by adding do-this-or-die mechanics.

Enshrouded knows that I, much like the family Golden Retriever, am treat-motivated. As long as there's shelter, fire, and decor, I'll get a stamina-boosting buff just by hanging out at home, but I'll never die from lack of sleep. In that regard, it's more like Valheim. Unique furnishings have their own comfort stats too, so there's incentive to explore Embervale for a new rug, fireplace, or even a toilet if you want a longer, more powerful boost. It's an especially exciting system for players like me, someone who loves building and decorating bases, but rarely sees a reward for the extra effort.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

All this meticulous decorating makes me wonder whether I really want Enshrouded to add enemy raids on player bases and risk destroying them, but I'm leaning toward yes. It's the one major survival mechanic I miss in its formula, and I can't help but wistfully remember how fun it is to scramble into action when Valheim warns, "The forest is moving..." Imagine that, but with Enshrouded's poisonous fog instead.

Enshrouded has always been my favorite survival-crafting block set, but I'm thrilled with the new build camera. Building in tight corners is less hassle, and I don't slide off the roof a dozen times..

There's got to be a high fantasy Ikea hidden somewhere in Embervale, because the amount of furniture and decor in Enshrouded is absurd. It's nice to go from picking at scraps to being overwhelmed by choice

Version 1.0 also added Sparkworks, a logic system for creating your own enemy spawns, player-triggered events, special world builds, custom dungeons, and more. Your creations are shareable, too, so other players can suffer through your cruel obstacle course designs. I've tinkered with it myself, but I've mostly spent my time exploring player-made hobbit holes and feeling painfully self-conscious by comparison.

Repetitive tasks—another hunt for a rare material, another trek across the map—can become exasperating even in the best survival crafting games. There's a thin line between tedium and satisfaction, and Enshrouded walks it better than most. Much of that is thanks to the game's philosophy around punishment and reward, but its RPG elements add a layer of complexity that more than makes up for anything missing from Enshrouded's "survival-lite" approach.

Take my group, for example. I play with seven other friends, while that feels like a lot for most survival crafting games, Enshrouded's combat roles give us distinctly useful jobs. Rather than dumping points into three or four barebones stats, your Flameborn can specialize across 12 different skill trees. I mostly opt for tank, athlete, and assassin perks, but my allies fill other needs with mix-and-match builds for glass-cannon wizards, battlemage healers, or stealthy assassins. We also have our preferred responsibilities, like mining, woodcutting, gardening, cooking, and all those other usual genre chores.

Enshrouded's boss fights are a blast and more dynamic than similar games. Fights aren't as mechanically heavy as a Conan Exiles dungeon boss, but the traditional tank-and-spank approach won't cut it.

Hollow Halls—Enshrouded's massive dungeons that practically demand group play—are where combat roles shine the most. I beat one playing solo, but also wiped several times in a group of four.

A word of caution: multiplayer groups of more than two or three people should consider a dedicated server. Version 1.0 significantly improves performance, but not enough to spare bigger parties from the occasional murderous lag spike.

Multiplayer is also where some of my biggest gripes with Enshrouded remain, and despite heavy reworks to its questing systems, my group still struggled to make sense of the journal when our objectives fell out of sync. Our confusion mostly stemmed from completing world progression quests without the full party, so when absent friends logged back in, their to-do list didn't look the same and they had a list of missed quests. There are separate, personal quests to do at your own leisure, but we constantly compared our journals to make sure no one had gone off course.

I'm still not sure if any of that even mattered. No one was ever locked out of crafting recipes or new biomes because of the discrepancies, so the punishment boiled down to a smidge of missed XP and simply missing out on the moment. It didn't end up being a big deal, and I'm starting to think the journal's 'missed quest' label made the whole thing feel more consequential than it actually was. I clenched my jaw in frustration a few times, but if that's my biggest nitpick, then Enshrouded is survival crafting gold.

There's got to be a high fantasy Ikea hidden somewhere in Embervale, because the amount of furniture and decor in Enshrouded is absurd.

As much as I love the genre, I can't pretend it isn't filled with seemingly eternal early access pits. I've played in plenty of messy sandboxes, a handful of good ones, and just a few great ones. Then there's Enshrouded, operating in a league of its own. But even then, Enshrouded isn't just a good survival crafting game: it's a damn good game by any measure. Its building tools reward even my most impractical ambitions, and I'll never grow tired of exploring Embervale's hidden nooks and crannies.

Few games in the genre match its distinct identity or degree of polish, and after 500+ hours of adventuring, there's little left to wish for. My biggest dilemma post-Enshrouded will be moving on from a survival crafting RPG so lovingly handcrafted. I fear Keen Games has cooked up something that has forever changed my palate.

The fog of war clears around Embervale, revealing a survival crafting masterpiece.

Andrea has been covering games for nearly a decade, picking up bylines at IGN, USA Today, Fanbyte, and Destructoid before joining the PC Gamer team in 2025. She's got a soft spot for older RPGs and is willing to try just about anything with a lovey-dovey "I can fix them" romance element. Her weekly to-do always includes a bit of MMO time, endlessly achievement hunting and raiding in Final Fantasy 14. Outside of those staples, she's often got a few survival-crafting games on rotation and loves a good scare in co-op horror games.

#3709. Six Things to Do Between Sets at the Gym

Rest is a crucial part of strength training. Depending on the exercise and your goals, you may find yourself resting 30 seconds, or one minute, or three to five minutes. So what do you actually do during that time? Let’s talk about your options, both in terms of training effectiveness and gym etiquette.

As awkward as it may feel at first, this is the best option for most people, most of the time. Actually rest. Don’t stretch, don’t work a different muscle; just allow your body to recover.

Some gyms will have stools, benches, or folding chairs near the platforms where people are lifting heavy (and thus need the longest rests). I’m mostly thinking of powerlifting and weightlifting gyms, but I’ve been to big-box gyms like Crunch that provide seating as well. And impromptu seats are common in many other places—who hasn’t sat on a plyo box or some other convenient surface?

There are plenty of little actions that you take at the gym (or should take) that are not explicitly exercise. The rest between sets is the perfect time to do these little maintenance tasks. Things like:

Change the weights to what you’ll need for your next set.

Write down what you just lifted in your notebook or lifting app.

If you took a video, watch it to give yourself feedback for the next set.

Trim that video so that you (or your coach, or your friends) don’t have to watch all 20 seconds of you fumbling with the camera and adjusting your belt before you actually lift.

Have a drink of water and, if needed, a snack.

Clean up after yourself! Rack any plates and dumbbells you aren’t using.

During the last few sets of an exercise, it’s time to start thinking about what you’ll do next. This could mean grabbing the equipment you’ll need or changing your shoes, but it's also an excellent opportunity to start warming up—especially if it’s an exercise that can benefit from a little gentle mobility work.

Let’s say you have a few sets of squats left, but after that you’ll do some overhead press. You probably want to warm up your shoulders with some mobility work so that you won’t be so tight when you hit that nice stable overhead position. Or maybe it’s the other way around, and you’re pressing, but next you’ll do squats. It’s a great time to start doing some ankle mobility work so that you’ll be able to comfortably hit a deeper squat.

When the weights are routine, I sit and chill. When they get heavy, I need to pace. (At weightlifting competitions, I not only stake out a warmup platform, I also pick out a walking path that I can pace between attempts.)

Or if you’re more of a cheerful, high-energy person, maybe you just want to dance. You’ll see this most often from people who lift at home, or at a chummy small gym where an impromptu dance party might occur between friends. Alone in my garage gym, I’ve been known to put on some good karaoke songs and sing along, with or without dancing.

The idea is not to get some extra cardio or get your steps in, but just to stay busy and loose and have fun—or, if you’re nervous about a big lift, to keep your head. At a busy commercial gym, make sure not to walk too far away, and consider leaving your water bottle or gym bag on your equipment to let people know it’s still taken.

I promise that it is actually OK to look at your phone between sets. You’re probably doing it anyway. There’s your lifting app, your videos that you took to check your squat form—and, yes, your usual texting and social media stuff.

The risk you’re taking here is that you’ll get distracted and rest too long. Too much rest, say more than 10 minutes, can make you feel both mentally and physically unprepared. Long rests can also lengthen your workout. Sticking to the minimum necessary rest times will get you in and out of the gym a lot faster.

From others’ perspective, a person who sits on a machine for 10 minutes scrolling is committing an unforgivable sin in gym etiquette. Don’t take longer rests than you need, if you’re holding up equipment. (That said, if you’re polite to others who approach, and you accept requests to “work in” (take turns) while you scroll, you’re morally in the clear.)

For your own sake, set a timer when you do anything that might distract you between sets. I like how I can program rest times into a Garmin watch workout, but Hevy also has a timer, and you can always use the regular timer function on your watch or phone.

Another tip: Be mindful about what you’re doing on your phone. Now is not the time to get into an argument on the internet, or check your work email and see what will be waiting for you back at the office. It is a good time to play little games on your phone, or read an ebook, or put together your next great workout playlist.

I’m leaving this option for last because I don’t want it to be your go-to. Just because you can do one exercise while resting for another, doesn’t mean you should.

Why not? If you really want to give squats your full energy, for example, don’t do pull-ups on the squat rack in between. You’ll fatigue yourself more than you realize, and you won’t do your best on those squats.

But supersets can be great if you’re willing to sacrifice a little weight for a lot of time. They’re best for exercises where the exact weight doesn’t matter—you can pair bicep curls with tricep extensions, or pull-ups with dips (so long as you’re a person who can bang out multiple reps of each with ease).

To do a superset, you just do a set of the first exercise, then a set of the second, then rest a short time (if needed at all), and repeat. I have a list of the best superset pairs here—usually you’ll want to do opposing muscles, like a push exercise with a pull exercise.

#3708. Yakuza creator's new studio and its debut game Gang of Dragon are no more after losing funding from NetEase

Nagoshi Studio has officially shut down and its first game called Gang of Dragon is seemingly no more, months after publisher NetEase pulled funding from the Yakuza-like project.

Toshihiro Nagoshi (often cited as the creator of the brilliant Yakuza and Like A Dragon game series) opened his new studio in 2021 and announced his next game with a very familiar title almost one year ago. Now, the Tokyo-based developer has closed its doors, as confirmed in the Japanese government gazette Kanpo.

The news comes months after employees were told that the studio's future was at risk due to NetEase's funding cuts. Nagoshi Studio reportedly needed another £33.1 million (about $44.4m at the time) to get Gang of Dragon past the finish line - a paycheck NetEase purportedly didn't want to cough up.

The China-based Marvel Rivals and Where Winds Meet publisher has been significantly scaling back on international investments these past few years. Visions of Mana developer Ouka Studios was shut down just after launching its gorgeous action game, Worlds Untold (a studio formed by Mass Effect veteran Mac Walters) had to pause operations to find a new partner, and Halo Infinite lead Jerry Hook's studio also ran into very similar issues last year.

Some developers have been a little luckier. Suda51's Grasshopper Manufacture saved itself with a management buyout and now operates as an independent developer, for one.

Not much is known about Gang of Dragon, but its debut trailer featured the violent crime and high drama you'd expect from Nagoshi's previous work. The game also starred Ma Dong-seok, the acclaimed actor you might recognise from films such as Train to Busan and Marvel's Eternals.

#3707. South Of Midnight Director Says He Doesn’t Think Xbox Should Have Funded It

Now free to pursue its own destiny independent of Xbox, South of Midnight developer Compulsion Games has been actively looking for collaborative work with other partners. But given some comments recently made by creative director David Sears, I wouldn’t be surprised if Compulsion’s next project was something very, very different from South of Midnight; after all, Sears doesn’t think that game was a great business decision to begin with.

In an interview with MinnMax‘s Ben Hanson, Sears speaks at length about Xbox’s decision to fund games like South of Midnight and Double Fine’s Keeper, games which he and Xbox knew would probably not make lots of money (and in fact did not) but would increase Xbox’s prestige, or serve as cultural cornerstones for generations to come. However, he also says that he told people during development, “Somebody is going to say, one day, ‘The money tap, we’re closing those floodgates.’ And that’s going to have really traumatic results downstream.”

Hanson then summarizes what he thinks Sears is saying. “So the idea is, you’re thankful that Microsoft supported the hell out of South of Midnight…but you would not have funded it yourself?”

Sears replied, “Yeah, probably.” He continued:

I wanted to make it. No doubt. Obviously. Because we made it. Would I have turned off someone else’s money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah. Because I’m not completely selfless. It just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable. Of course it was going to have a “shocking” outcome. It’s easy to dissect it now. But at the time, I would talk to other directors and [they’d] be like, “How is this happening? How did we get so lucky? Is this a golden era?” And I’d always be like (he sucks in air through his teeth) “For now.” And there’s always a night when Rome burns. I didn’t know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it.

Sears concludes this thought by remarking that the Microsoft of today is much “more humane” than the company he knew in the ’90s, as demonstrated by the fact that it let studios spin off in the first place instead of just shutting them down entirely.

In addition to South of Midnight, Compulsion Games is also known for 2018’s We Happy Few, which it made with Gearbox Publishing. It was acquired by Microsoft just ahead of that release to join Xbox Game Studios, and began working on South of Midnight, which was nominated for and won numerous awards after its launch in 2025, including a BAFTA. Compulsion was spun out from Microsoft as a part of Xbox’s recent restructuring, taking with it all its IP and an unknown amount of financial runway. It’s currently unknown whether or not the studio has signed a new project yet.

Few movie franchises have had the cultural impact of the James Bond movies. Generations grew up watching 007 on the big screen (with the movies currently streaming with an Amazon Prime subscription), and all eyes are on what Denis Villeneuve will do with the developing 26th film. Specifically, who will play James. There are a number of names being tossed around online, and someone recently asked Jack Lowden about taking up the martini and pistol as the beloved MI6 agent.

No Time To Die's tragic ending brought an end to Daniel Craig's Bond movies, opening the door for someone else to take the mantle. Folks have been taking bets on who might play Bond next, and Lowden is just one such choice. In an interview with GQ he was asked about the online discourse, saying:

On this… It’s all very flattering. It’s nice to be mentioned – for any role – and I’m just not really going to add to the noise.

While he's not adding his own commentary to the situation, it sounds like Lowden has seen Gary Oldman's comments that he's on the shortlist to play 007. He seems to appreciate anyone considering him for a major role, yet alone something as big as James Bond. We'll just have to see who ends up playing that iconic character next, and whether or not it's the Slow Horses star.

Later in the same interview, Jack Lowden spoke more about his career, and aging in the entertainment industry. The actor, who is now 36 years old, spoke about his age changes the way people perceive him. When asked by the journalist about reaching the era when "You either become a leading man or you don't," Lowden said this:

I count myself lucky, in that I’ve had a relatively gradual build. So I’ve been allowed to develop as a man, as a person, outside the spotlight. It’s funny – you go from being ‘a bright young thing’ to just ‘a thing’.

Luckily that process has opened him up to new roles, and now he's a popular choice online to replace Daniel Craig as 007. Whether or not he actually get passed the baton remains to be seen, but the fact that he's allegedly on the short list is a testament to his talent and starpower.

As a reminder, Oldman's comments about Lowden came from an appearance on Global TV’s The Morning Show . He gushed about his Slow Horses co-star possibly getting the role saying:

It’s been rumored that [Jack] is on the shortlist. We’re going to find out pretty soon, aren’t we? Because they have picked him. They have made their choice, but they have not announced it yet. So my fingers are crossed for Jack.

Clearly Lowden has Oldman's endorsement. Now that I think of it, it's surprising that the Oppenheimer actor never actually appeared in a Bond movie. I feel like he would have been a great antagonist for 007, especially considering his villainous roles in projects like Lost in Space and (especially) Air Force One. My FOMO is through the roof.

While we wait for Bond 26 casting news, folks can watch Slow Horses on Apple TV as part of the 2026 TV schedule. We'll just have to see if Oldman gets his wish and his co-star gets to land the career-changing role.

I tried the demo for Queen's Domain last year and liked it a lot⁠—though it definitely had some friction I wasn't sure about. The full game launched on October 30, and I eagerly rushed through the parts I'd already played in the demo.

Turns out, that demo cut out right when things were about to go nuts.

Five hours in out of an estimated 30+, and Queen's Domain is easily one of my top games of the year. I am only begrudgingly writing this, because I'd rather be playing right now.

Queen's Domain starts out resembling other entries in a growing subgenre of indie King's Field-likes, paying homage to the first-person dark fantasy RPG series FromSoftware put out before its soulsward turn. In its first half hour or so, Queen's Domain distinguishes itself similarly to fellow genre standout Lunacid: Fantastic art, maybe even better music, and a mastery of nostalgic intangibles (menu, UI, sound cues, etc.) After beating the first boss, Queen's Domain rewards you with a magic airdash sword, and it's at that point that the game truly begins.

Queen's Domain is a very deliberately paced game and, like a lot of first-person RPGs, it starts out feeling like your boots will always be on the ground. Think the difference between Doom and Quake: You can mostly tell when a game will let you get some air or not.

But once I was rocking the Holy Sword, Endu? Holy shit. Queen's Domain's first area opens up like some wonderful clockwork contraption. A lot of the verticality reminds me of Destiny raids, the way hidden paths blend into the environment, and reaching them feels like you're sequence breaking.

Endu can be upgraded with special gems throughout the game, with each giving you an extra dash while airborne. I'm up to three at the time of writing, and each upgrade has felt like it radically opened up my traversal options: There are parts of the first few maps I'm pretty sure I'll only be able to reach once I'm up to four or five dashes, zooming from one end of the map to the other without touching the ground.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Endu's a standout, but it's not the only tool available: Queen's Domain seems to have an expansive arsenal, and weapons can transform as they're upgraded. You upgrade weapons just by using them, and the game has no stat allocation on level up, encouraging experimentation with the arsenal⁠—PC Gamer hardware writer James Bentley managed to max upgrade 20 weapons across his full playthrough. You can effectively create a "build" via your choice of which weapons to hotkey (limit of three) and upgrade, a system that more resembles BioShock or the System Shock Remake rather than something like Dark Souls or Lunacid.

My favorite alongside Endu so far has been the Caestus, a type of medieval knuckle duster that's been a standby of the Souls games. Here, it's a fast-attacking blunt weapon useful against slashing-resistant skeletons. Instead of a horizontal dash like Endu, its special attack is an uppercut that launches my character into the air. Plenty of fun to use on enemies, but I've loved deploying it as an effective double jump to reach otherwise-inaccessible areas⁠—and there's always been a surprise or meaningful reward waiting for me when I do.

My coworker, PCG staff writer Morgan Park, initially bounced off the pre-Endu, demo-equivalent portion of Queen's Domain. I'm here to say stay strong, prayer warriors. It is worth getting through that first half hour. While there's something to be said about it potentially putting new players off, I think the contrast between pre-and post-Endu gameplay is so strong, it makes the air dash feel all the more powerful. You know what it's like to be stuck on the ground, and you won't take it for granted.

It's the sort of contrast metroidvanias thrive on⁠—I always think of how dinky you feel before you get the wall jump in Hollow Knight⁠—and Queen's Domain's brilliant level design might leave it the best first-person metroidvania anyone's made since the first Metroid Prime.

And I think Prime's a strong comparison point overall here: The cryptic atmosphere, breathtaking vistas, and genuinely unique approach to first-person movement and level design speak to that. I'm already seeing hints toward game-spanning backtracking in my future, but I've got reason to suspect Queen's Domain's backtracking will be less frustrating and obtuse than Metroid Prime's.

I already love this game, and I am about to mainline it over the next 30 hours or so of my free time⁠—stay tuned for our full Queen's Domain review to come. Meanwhile, Queen's Domain is available on Steam for a launch price of $17, down from an MSRP of $20.

#3704. A Scam Website Is Trying To Cash In On AO3 Outage By ‘Selling’ Audiobooks Of Fanfics

In an attempt to prey on individuals bereft of free things to readÂ in the wake of the massive AO3 outage, a new website has seemingly popped up out of the ether, promising readers all their favorite fanfictions and the authors of said fanfics a bit of cash. The website, AO3.life (which I will not link to for reasons that will become apparent soon) purports to be the salvation of the actual AO3, the fanfiction website which was recently taken offline after a security incident and may remain down for weeks. This new website appears to have scraped a cached version of AO3, as users report older versions of their work on it, as well as works that have been deleted or made private.

The fact that this site uses AO3’s name and hosts an outdated, unauthorized version of the fanfiction website, one where works have been reposted without the authors’ consent, is bad enough. But there’s also the stank of scam permeating ao3.life. The website claims that it pays authors by selling their works as audiobooks with the proceeds split, “91% to the author, 9% to ao3.life.” All you have to do, the site claims, to either receive your cash or to remove your fics from this felonious-ass site is send them an email from the account tied to your AO3 profile.

For the love of the omegaverse, do not do this.

As many users on social media have pointed out, this is an elaborate phishing/doxxing attempt. The Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the parent non-profit behind AO3, is aware of the situation and is taking steps to get the site taken down. On the AO3 subreddit, a moderator posted a message from OTW being sent to users reporting ao3.life. “We are aware and are taking action, but please be patient because the legal system is much slower than online life,” it read.

#3703. You Can Now Lock Your Private ChatGPT Conversations With a PIN

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you have personal conversations with ChatGPT that you don't want others to see, you can now add an extra layer of security for those specific chats. The new Locked Chats feature allows you to hide sensitive conversations behind a four-digit account PIN (or biometric authentication on mobile), meaning others with access to your device or screen can't read them.

Locked chats are retained in your chat history—unlike temporary chats, which are private conversations that aren't saved by default—so you can return to or continue them at any point. However, once locked, they are hidden from your regular chat history, pinned chats, and regular conversation search. To access them, you have to go to Projects > Locked chats and enter your PIN or device unlock method (such as Face ID or Touch ID).

To start a locked chat for the first time, open an existing conversation that you want to keep private and open the options menu. Select Lock chat > Lock chat and create or enter your account PIN. This moves the conversation to your locked chats project. You can repeat this with any existing conversation or start a locked chat from scratch under Projects > Locked Chats by entering your PIN or authentication method and typing a message to launch the chat. When you're done, select Lock now to end access to locked chats and hide them from the sidebar.

Note that if you don't already have an account PIN set up, you should be prompted to do so the first time you attempt to lock a chat. Select Create a PIN, enter your four-digit code, and enter it again to confirm. You can also enable biometric authentication in Account PIN settings. If you reset your account PIN at any point, all locked chats are permanently deleted and cannot be recovered.

Locked chats are available on ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans on both mobile and desktop apps. The feature is not available for ChatGPT for Healthcare. There are other limitations, too: For example, temporary, archived, and group chats can't be locked, nor can those with shared links, scheduled and background tasks, or meeting recordings. OpenAI says locked chats are rolling out gradually, so they may not be available to all users yet.

#3702. GOG Explains How One Of The Most Important PC Games Ever Made Is Trapped In Licensing Hell

Westwood Studios’ Dune 2: The Building of a Dynasty isn’t the first real-time strategy game ever made, but it is one of the earliest examples of the genre and essentially provided the blueprint for what RTS games would be moving forward, inspiring Blizzard and other studios in the process. But it seems very unlikely that this important bit of PC gaming history will get an official re-release anytime soon or be part of GOG’s preservation program.Â

In a new interview with GamesRadar, Marcin Paczynski, senior business development and partnerships manager at PC gaming store GOG, explained just how complicated and messy the rights are to 1992’s Dune 2. And it comes down to the influential RTS being based on a movie based on a book, from a studio owned by another company; in this case, EA.

“So currently, Electronic Arts has the game code, the assets, all of the rights to those things, and all the materials around the game,” explained Paczynski.

“But of course, they do not own the [Dune] IP. The problem with the IP is that it is not directly owned by [Dune writer Frank Herbert’s estate], because the games were not based on the books; they were actually based on the movie from 1984. That movie was created by Universal Pictures, and the main producer for that movie was [Dino De Laurentiis]. The problem is that he also has part of that movie license with him. But he died 15 years ago.”

That means De Laurentiis’ estate owns a “portion” of Dune 2. And then there’s another complication. Legendary Pictures owns the IP rights for the new Dune movies and has a deal with Funcom to create Dune Awakening, a survival gameÂ set in the Dune universe. And according to Paczynski, there’s some amount of “exclusivity” included in that deal.

Exactly how or even if that deal would get in the way of re-releasing Westwood’s classic Dune games, including Dune 2000, is “currently not clear,” says Paczynski. But it’s yet one more issue to deal with if anyone were to try to bring back these important classics.

For Paczynski, this is likely a frustrating situation as he considers Dune 2 as one of his personal “holy grails” for GOG to bring back and preserve.

“It’s on the top of my list, my personal one, because this is a game that I have a lot of nostalgia for,” said Paczynski. “The situation is a good example of how bad it can get with the licensing situation of a game.”

It’s also a great example of why fan projects tend to be the betterâand often onlyâoption for playing classic games decades after launch. Fans making patches and mods don’t (generally) have to deal with lawyers and legal hurdles in the same way GOG and other companies have to when trying to bring back a classic.

Still, I hope one day Dune 2 is given a proper, officially supported re-release on modern PC storefronts so it can be easily played by new gamers. Dune essentially ushered in what would become the modern RTS and, as a result, led to the creation of games like Warcraft, which then led to MOBAs like League of Legends. It’s an important piece of gaming history that deserves a return.

It’s hard to believe now there was a time when Steve Carell was not a veteran in this industry. He really kicked things off with The Daily Show during Jon Stewart’s run and was on a long list of big names who came through The Daily Show in its heyday on Comedy Central. This includes some heavy hitters like John Oliver, Samantha Bee, Hasan Minhaj, Ed Helms, and more. It was Carell though who spoke out about his time on The Daily Show and how some Star Trek fans and Stephen Colbert helped him find his footing on TV.

Apparently, whilst working together it was Colbert who gave Steve Carell some prime (and frankly fascinating) advice. It was in the late nineties that both Hollywood personalities joined Jon Stewart on The Daily Show, but Colbert had a couple of years on Carell when he signed on – though Carell previously said on The Late Show it was also Colbert who got him hired by Comedy Central.

From what the actor told Amy Poehler, he was having a little trouble figuring out how to make the gig work when Colbert gave him the key to opening up the world of news satire.

I know Colbert, Stephen, gave me great advice, which was, ‘Come up with a character, and that will make it that much more palatable.’ My character was someone who didn’t quite understand, didn’t quite get it, but was super serious about everything he was asking.

If you ever saw The Colbert Report, you should know this is the approach Stephen Colbert himself took, but I didn’t realize it was advice he was cultivating in a little petri dish and then decimating out into the Comedy Central world when newbies needed it.

This is where Star Trek comes in. As someone who works with quite a few Trek fans, I’m aware of how passionate and positive they can be, and how much they like to fill up convention Halls at places like San Diego Comic-Con. Apparently, Carell at the time was not. The actor told Amy Poehler on her “Good Hang” podcast that he realized how helpful being able to turn the joke on himself could be during none other than a Star Trek fan convention.

It was while talking to people at a Klingon speakers convention that he realized making fun of these people who were so passionate about the franchise they boldly went where few other fans had gone and learned the language was not the way to move forward. Carell likened the hobby to “woodworking” or “photography” and when he got to the convention he realized The Daily Show shouldn’t be mocking these fans.

I remember doing one field piece which were, it was a Klingon speakers convention. You know, you go and obviously the idea is ‘Let’s make fun of people who meet and learn how to speak Klingon.’ And they were the nicest, gentlest, I really liked these people a lot. … And I thought, ‘No, it has to be about what an idiot I am.’

Steve Carell would later leave The Daily Show to take the lead in The Office. He’s had both a movie and TV career in the decades that followed, and he's among the more recognizable names in Hollywood these days. Regardless, it’s easy to see another path that could have been taken: one where he took the easy route and mocked the Star Trek fans, one where he didn’t create “a character” that later resonated with audiences. One that may never have led the man to bigger and better things. I don’t know if Carell’s ever thanked Stephen Colbert for that little nugget of wisdom, but it was certainly helpful advice.

She now uses those skills in researching and tracking down information in very different ways.

#3700. Creativity Is Conning Us

We are culturally obsessed with innovation. Consider TED Talks and Apple’s “Think Different” campaign and our obsession with tech founder-philosophers. The writer Thomas Frank has. In The Creativity Con: How Innovation Became America’s Biggest Racket, the author deconstructs what he calls “our national fascination with creativity.” The book has chapters on neoliberalism, AI, and the current concept of the creative class. His research included a long trip to a music festival turned marketing love-in, South by Southwest, which he describes in his smart, dry way as a “marathon trade show with something like 40,000 attendees” and “a more inclusive, more lovable version of Davos.”

Frank, who is 61 and lives in Maryland, is best known for his bestselling books about politics, including What’s the Matter With Kansas? and Listen, Liberal. But his new book is in some ways a belated sequel to his first book, 1997’s The Conquest of Cool, about how advertising co-opted the rhetoric of the 1960s counterculture to sell us Pepsi and cars. (It’s the kind of book you’ll think of often: anytime you see the launch of a new extreme energy drink and still required reading for anyone doing a Mad Men rewatch.)

Since Frank’s newest work focuses on creativity and innovation as the drivers of American affluence, I thought meeting him on his book tour for slop bowls at Sweetgreen, a salad marketed as an efficient and innovative way to get a nutritious meal, would be apropos. But the Sweetgreen on the Upper East Side was both loud and had nowhere to sit, a sad reflection of how Americans view workday lunches. Luckily, a small Vietnamese restaurant on Lexington Avenue became a welcome space for bahn mi and a discussion of the great man theory, the midterm elections, and using AI for gardening advice.

This interview has been condensed for length and clarity.

Vanity Fair: I can’t believe you were at South by Southwest for nine whole days researching this book.

Thomas Frank: Longer. It goes for 10 days, and I was determined to see the whole thing.

Did it make you depressed, or what was your takeaway?

Well, I was fascinated. That was one of the first things I did for the book. It was March of ’23. So, you know, I—I had my theories and my ideas and my preconceived notions, and I was like, “What? What am I going to find?” I wasn’t prepared at all for what swept over me.

One of my favorite parts of the whole book is that the CIA was there at the Creative Industries Expo.

I love that when they asked you if you had any questions you asked them a spicy question about the JFK assassination. What else did you do early on for research?

I went back and read [Thomas] Carlyle, On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History. That is where he introduced the great man theory of history. He thinks the nature of humanity is to worship heroes, and that sort of gave rise to this sort of whole genius theory. So I didn’t talk about any of this in the book—it all got left on the cutting room floor—but then in the 19th century, they had this theory of the great genius, that Franz Liszt or Napoleon or Goethe had this spark and we had to sort of honor them. And they were quasi-magical, because we couldn’t really understand how they did it. And that obviously rubs Americans the wrong way. Even though our democracy is falling to pieces, we are an intensely egalitarian people.

How did you decide what to cover and keep in the book?

The way I decided to do the book was historical and then sociological. So I did the historical part, and a lot of it is [about] Obama and Reagan. And then for the sociological part, I decided I would choose a state and describe the innovation initiatives there. And I chose Maryland because I live there. I chose an industry, and the one I chose is the defense contractors.

Defense contractors love to talk about how innovative they are. There are like five industries that really abuse this language [of innovation]: defense, advertising, pharma, the tech guys, and Wall Street.

What is the creepiest thing you learned about defense contractors?

The contrast between what they make and the way they describe it, which is wholesome all-American innovation. It’s language that’s just camouflage.

You’ve written a lot about politics. Do you think there’s going to be a big midterm shift happening?

The country is definitely turning against Trump. But then again, what do I know? The polls have been so wrong all these years. I mean look, the Iran war is so unpopular, and it’s really unpopular with the very people that voted for him.

They have to have something that they stand for, and it can’t be innovation.

Oh yeah, absolutely. The Republicans used to love the language of creativity, and the Democrats liked the language of innovation. So [President] Carter used to talk about innovation all the time, and at the same time, Reagan was always talking about creativity. Nobody said at the time, “this is a battle between innovation and creativity.”

How do you define the difference between innovation and creativity?

Technically, innovation has to do with actually producing a product. Creativity means facility with art and language. But in practice, the words overlap all the time and are used as synonyms. They were basically synonyms and then split back in the ’60s when creativity was identified with the counterculture, and innovation was identified with engineers, military, industrial, and technology. And the counterculture really turned against all of that stuff.

It’s funny that after all of your political books, this one still ends with Trump.

Yeah, Trump and AI. The last chapter is all about it.

I have no technical understanding of it, so I wouldn’t know. I don’t think anybody else knows either because it’s all private. It’s proprietary. I compare it to a private sector Manhattan project. My wife is an economist. She finds it extremely useful. In my work for this book, it was not useful.

I’m really into gardening, and it’s very helpful with gardening. It’s very helpful with household chores. It knows a lot about stereo equipment.

#3696. Karen Bass on Nithya Raman, Her Radical Past, and the Fight to Remain LA Mayor

Karen Bass was showing me her three iPhones when I visited her at Getty House, the official residence of the Los Angeles mayor, late last month. One was her personal phone, another was for government business, and the third had been hacked so many times that she wasn’t supposed to use it anymore. But Bass couldn’t bring herself to ditch the number, which she’s had for 20 years, because friends and colleagues still call it. So she kept the compromised phone around, monitoring its incessant ringing during our interview.

Bass, 73, has the warmth of a grandmother who wants to make sure you’re hydrated, and, as I discovered, the authority of a disappointed matriarch who expects you to know better. The intimidating part is that she can vacillate between those two sides of herself rather quickly.

With a disarming smile, she offered me a glass of water and invited me to meet her daughter and grandson, who live with her at Getty House.

Bass photographed at the Getty House in Los Angeles, September 2026.

But when I suggested that Bass, a lifelong progressive who has traveled to Fidel Castro’s Cuba to study alternatives to capitalism, was borrowing from the conservative playbook to portray her opponent Nithya Raman as a dangerous extremist, a different side of Bass came out. Suddenly I was sitting across from a stern political veteran who had little patience for people challenging her judgment.

“That’s not true,” she shot back defensively.

I mentioned a campaign email that I thought implied Raman might be antisemetic. Bass and an aide disputed my characterization, insisting that the campaign has simply criticized Raman for skipping a Jewish heritage event at City Hall.

Did she believe Raman was antisemetic? “I don’t know what she is,” Bass replied. “It depends on the time of day and day of the week.”

At one point when I asked whether she would warn her successor about the city’s dysfunctional homelessness bureaucracy, Bass took another swipe at Raman.

“Well, if she’s my successor, no, she knows it all,” Bass said with a sarcastic undertone.

Just four years ago Bass was embraced by the local progressive movement in LA. But now she’s getting flak from both sides of the political spectrum and finds herself courting conservative voters to defeat Raman, who is running to the left of Bass.

For over a year, wealthy donors have been trying to find her replacement. Rick Caruso, the billionaire developer who spent more than $100 million trying to defeat Bass in 2022, says he was encouraged by Ari Emanuel and former Governor Jerry Brown to consider another run for elected office. Spencer Pratt, the reality television villain whose house burned down in the Palisades fire, transformed his personal tragedy into an insurgent mayoral campaign, attracting wealthy Hollywood supporters and massive amounts of attention on social media that was driven by his atypical political ads and AI-generated promotional videos made by his supporters.

But neither man became Bass’s 2026 general-election opponent. Instead, the challenge came from the left, in the form of Raman, a Harvard-educated democratic socialist who even endorsed the mayor’s reelection before entering the race. Now Bass finds herself vying for Pratt supporters on the right. She’s made public safety—an issue Pratt harped on—central to her reelection campaign, and has tried to paint Raman as soft on crime. Raman is also making a play for Pratt supporters, even invoking Ronald Reagan at the beginning of the only televised debate between the two candidates since June’s primary.

Bass is even showing up with Caruso on the campaign trail now. The two appeared together this month at the developer’s luxury shopping mall in the Pacific Palisades in what amounted to an unlikely reunion given Caruso’s unflattering assessment of her leadership. “People feel let down by the city,” he told me in August. Caruso also argued that LA mayors have more power than they care to admit. “They do have enough power and they don’t use it right,” he said. But perhaps Caruso sees Bass as a more palatable option than Raman, who carries the weight of a DSA association. Caruso called the socialist organization’s platform “dangerous” and said he would be voting for Bass in the upcoming election.

Karen Bass and Rick Caruso talk while on a tour of his shopping center, Palisades Village, in the Pacific Palisades, October 20, 2026.

A September UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll conducted for the Los Angeles Times found Raman leading Bass 39% to 28% among likely voters, with another 33% undecided. Nearly two thirds of respondents viewed Bass unfavorably. The numbers were hardly conclusive (no polls are these days), but they laid bare the fact that a politician who entered City Hall with considerable goodwill is now facing a difficult fight for another term. Bass could very well become the first Los Angeles mayor in 21 years not to be given a second term. If she wins, it’ll likely be because a lot of Pratt primary voters decided she was the lesser of two evils.

It’s a bit of an ironic situation that Bass finds herself in. Before she was mayor, before she was a congresswoman, before she became Speaker of the California state assembly, she was a teenage radical who considered running for public office an act of ideological surrender.

“Running for office was selling out,” she recalled when we spoke at a Croatian community center in San Pedro.

Has she changed? Or, like Reagan before her, has the increasingly left-leaning Democratic Party left her behind?

Bass was 14 when she signed her mother up to serve as a precinct captain for Robert F. Kennedy’s presidential campaign, she tells me. Her mother didn’t actually do the work. Bass did, riding her bicycle to campaign headquarters and immersing herself in the senator’s bid for the White House.

She was supposed to attend Kennedy’s primary-victory celebration at the Ambassador Hotel in June 1968, but her parents wouldn’t let her go because it was a school night.

“So I listened to the assassination on the radio,” she says.

The murder was devastating to Bass and her parents. Just two months earlier, Martin Luther King Jr. had been assassinated and, to Bass’s parents, it seemed like anyone involved in progressive politics would suffer the same fate.

“I was like, ‘It’s over.’ I was done,” she says. “I became much more interested in antiestablishment work.”

Her parents were reluctant to let her dive into politics. But the young Bass had already been politicized. Growing up in Los Angeles, she encountered the contradictions of establishment liberal politics. She attended Hamilton High School, which she says was predominantly Jewish, with roughly 300 Black students among its 3,000 pupils, and witnessed white flight as Black families moved into previously segregated neighborhoods.

Bass surrounded by supporters during a press conference to kick off the next phase of her reelection campaign in Los Angeles, June 9, 2026.

“It was painful,” she said. “Very confusing for a child because, you know, I’m talking Martin Luther King and all this stuff, and they’re like, ‘Oh no, not here.’”

She went on to become deeply involved in the anti-apartheid movement and learned how to organize from older activists. But by the late 1980s, she was growing increasingly frustrated with the distance between the political debates consuming her fellow activists and the violence engulfing South Central Los Angeles. The crack epidemic devastated neighborhoods, gang violence was killing young people, and elected officials only seemed to be interested in filling prisons. On the other end of the spectrum, she felt that progressive activists were more interested in relitigating the Iran-Contra scandal than they were in providing concrete relief to those suffering.

“I felt like what [progressive activists] were doing politically was theoretical and aspirational, but people were dying,” Bass says.

She quit her secure job teaching nursing at USC and founded the Community Coalition, an organization devoted to confronting addiction, violence, and poverty.

Her career change pissed off a lot of her compatriots. Bass was entering the nonprofit world, where she would have to negotiate with government agencies and accept money from the very institutions she had spent years protesting.

“I did the ultimate sellout move,” she jokes. “I took federal funding to start the organization.”

“I wanted to make a difference in people’s lives,” she says, “and my trajectory since then has been pragmatic, which has gotten me on the outs of some folks on the left. But that’s okay. As long as I’m delivering for poor people, I’m okay.”

Homelessness was Bass’s first priority when she was elected mayor. She left a secure seat in Congress to run for mayor in 2022, promising to confront the crisis with the urgency of a community organizer. It wasn’t hard to sell that vision to voters. She had experience tackling the crisis from her time at the Community Coalition.

Her signature program, Inside Safe, was designed to move people out of encampments and into temporary housing, where they could receive services and eventually secure permanent homes. For Bass, the program is evidence that her administration has made progress on an issue that befuddled her predecessors.

But the numbers tell a more complicated story. Street homelessness has declined over the course of her administration, but the city’s unsheltered population increased nearly 8% in the most recent annual count. In Raman’s council district, meanwhile, street homelessness fell roughly 49% during the same year.

Mayor Karen Bass during a debate with City Councilmember Nithya Raman with moderators from NBC4 and Telemundo 52, October 13, 2026.

Bass claims that the deeper problem is a fragmented homelessness bureaucracy. Under the current system, the city, county, and Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority share responsibilities, making it difficult to track spending and hold anyone accountable.

She wants to give the city greater authority over its own homelessness programs. But one might ask why she wasn’t able to give the city more power to fight the problem during her first term? She says her time was monopolized by moving people off the streets, and that she couldn’t simultaneously overhaul the bureaucratic inefficiencies at the homelessness agencies.

“I had to build the plane and fly it,” she tells me.

When I asked her to grade her performance on homelessness, she gave herself a B-plus. It was a confident assessment for a mayor whose signature issue became one of her most glaring political vulnerabilities during the primary. Pratt flooded the internet with videos and pictures portraying a homelessness crisis that was out of control. Whether it’s true or not that the problem got worse under Bass’s leadership was irrelevant. Pratt convinced large swaths of the city that it had.

Nothing has damaged Bass’s political standing more than the January 2025 wildfires.

When the Palisades fire erupted, the mayor was in Ghana as part of a presidential delegation. By the time she returned, the disaster had become a defining crisis of her administration.

The fire killed 12 people and destroyed thousands of homes. It also transformed the city’s politics, elevating figures such as Pratt, who lost his home and made the government’s response central to his mayoral campaign.

Bass has acknowledged that leaving Los Angeles was a mistake.

“My biggest regret was not being here,” she told me.

Bass maintains that the emergency notifications she would ordinarily have expected from public safety officials did not reach her before she left for Africa. But in the week leading up to the fires, weather forecasters were warning that the city could experience an extreme fire event. Companies were telling their employees to be safe. And news organizations were already planning how to cover the potential fires.

Bass knows that the mayor bears ultimate political responsibility, but she resists the idea that every institutional failure can be reduced to her negligence.

“Any time I made any attempts to explain, it was viewed as I was giving excuses and pointing fingers,” she says.

And yet Bass says she understands the anger of fire survivors.

“I understood and understand people’s anger because when you grieve, it is helpful if there’s somewhere that you could say, ‘This wouldn’t have happened except for that.’”

Bass is deeply familiar with the anger that comes with grief.

In 2006 her daughter Emilia and son-in-law Michael Wright were killed in a car accident. Bass told me about the painful impulse she felt to imagine how things might have turned out differently. For some time she wondered if she could have prevented their deaths.

“That was the absolute positively worst thing that could ever happen to me,” she says. “So consequently, everything since then, I feel like the worst has already happened. Nothing else could happen worse to me. Nothing.”

At Getty House, Bass tells me that she’s not going to read the state report on last year’s wildfires until it’s released to the public. She’s been accused of meddling in the LA Fire Department’s after-action report, published in October of last year, and she explained that she doesn’t want to be accused again of influencing or watering down the findings. For what it’s worth, she also said she hasn’t read the fire department’s report either.

“I have not seen it, and you know what? I don’t want to see it,” she says of a preview of the state report.

Bass’s relationship with Hollywood has soured a bit since she first took office. Meanwhile, it appears that much of the city’s creative class is siding with Raman, whose husband is an accomplished television writer who worked on 30 Rock and Modern Family.

Bass pushed for a settlement between state attorneys general and Paramount Skydance over an antitrust lawsuit that threatened to derail the company’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery after Paramount Skydance chief David Ellison indicated that he would move Paramount’s operations out of Los Angeles. She insists she wasn’t asking the AGs to approve the transaction. She says she just wanted to end the uncertainty hanging over the entertainment industry, which was already struggling to prevent runaway productions.

Bass says she spoke with Ellison while the lawsuit was active. She told me she was dissatisfied with the assurances he offered about preserving jobs over the next five years. But she worried that prolonged regulatory uncertainty would only compound the industry’s troubles.

The distinction mattered to Bass: She wasn’t necessarily taking the billionaire’s side, she argued. She was trying to protect the workers whose livelihoods depended on the outcome.

Bass’s budget management has also been a hot topic during campaign season, particularly the raises she negotiated for Los Angeles Police Department officers.

“She gave the police more money than they asked for, and then we had a $1 billion budget deficit [at the end of the 2024-2025 fiscal year],” says comedian and Raman supporter Adam Conover.

When Raman attacked her on this issue during the debate, Bass responded by saying her opponent was being disingenuous. “You know that some of these [fiscal management] problems have taken place over many decades,” Bass snapped back. “Frankly, it’s dishonest.”

Bass, then a Congresswoman, at a rally with then-mayor Antonio Villaraigosa in Los Angeles, California, March 23, 2011.

Then there is the downtown convention center.

The city is undertaking an approximately $2.6 billion expansion project intended to attract conferences and revive economic activity downtown.

Jason Oppenheim, the luxury real estate broker and Selling Sunset personality, sees the convention center project as an effort by the Bass administration to satisfy the unions—a very influential constituency in this city.

Oppenheim is hardly a natural ally of the DSA, but he has found himself increasingly intrigued by Raman.

“She strikes me as pragmatic and willing to go against her political base when necessary,” he tells me. “But I think a lot of people are more scared of the DSA than they are frustrated with Karen Bass’s tenure,” he says.

Oppenheim was getting a manicure when we spoke. He had not settled on a candidate yet, but he seemed at peace with the possibility of taking a political gamble.

“I don’t take risks on my nails,” he said. “I will on the mayor, but not on my manicures.”

The mayor wakes up between four and five in the morning and reads the Los Angeles Times, The New York Times, and international news outlets. The teenage activist who followed liberation movements around the world still has a fascination with foreign policy. She tells me she’s not too big a fan of her local paper these days because of how much ink it’s spilled criticizing her administration.

Bass spoke with unhoused people at an encampment during an Inside Safe operation in Los Angeles, September 26, 2024.

The mayor regularly attends Black churches, especially during campaign season. At a Pratt campaign event in South Central LA held in May, two women sitting in lawn chairs told me they were likely voting for Bass because she had recently attended their church for a Sunday service. Two more women at a community trash cleanup in the same neighborhood this October told me they were also voting for Bass because of her relationship to the neighborhood and its faith institutions.

When she was 14, Bass believed the system had failed. At 73, she believes the system can work if someone with sufficient experience and determination is running it.

Bass is not particularly impressed by the younger generation of progressive activists in Los Angeles.

“I don’t feel like there’s a real appreciation or thirst for history of past movements to learn past lessons,” she said.

She sees the Democratic Socialists of America as having the arguments that consumed earlier generations, particularly over whether ideological compromise is a betrayal or a necessary condition of achieving anything.

“At this point I stand for getting stuff done,” she told me. “I’ve always been a progressive, always supported social justice. That is a through line in my life from childhood to now.”

Bass also has a theory about what happens to young radicals as they get older. They have children and parenthood tempers their ideological purity with the practical demands of raising a family. The activists who once demanded radical change begin worrying about their children’s safety, their schools, and whether the neighborhood is a decent place to grow up. Their priorities change.

Of course Bass doesn’t see her own evolution as a retreat from her youthful convictions. She says the goals remain the same. But these days she’s working from within the system to achieve them.

The hard part for Bass will be convincing the voters who believe the system has failed them to choose her. And it leaves Bass in an uncomfortable position for a former radical: she’s defending the virtues of experience against a younger, more ideological candidate who believes Los Angeles needs something different.

Bass knows she might not get another four years to implement her policies. Even her staffers seem genuinely unsure of how election day will play out.

“Losing an election would be devastating,” she told me.

It felt like a big admission from a politician who usually projects confidence. However, Bass has endured worse than political defeat.

“There is no comparison of a parent losing a child to losing an election.”

#3694. Xbox’s Recent Efforts Haven’t Changed Anything And The Future Remains Bleak, Expert Says

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has undertaken a number of efforts thus far to help get the business back into a healthy place, and nothing has worked, Circana analyst Mat Piscatella says.

He told The Game Business that based on the sales and engagement data he sees for the US gaming industry, "I'm not seeing [the moves] have any positive impact" for Xbox.

The disc-to-digital program "hasn't changed their sales of new physical software trend at all," he added. Additionally, making Gears of War: E-Day exclusive on console to Xbox "hasn't made any difference" in terms of selling more Xbox hardware. In fact, Xbox sales continue to spiral. Sharma says there is a supply issue, but, in the US at least, you can get a new Xbox very easily.

Piscatella said E-Day is a "Gears-ass Gears of War game," and a gorgeous one. But making it exclusive to Xbox created a scenario where "you chop the legs out" from under its potential potential to boost Xbox generally. "At least in the short term, it hasn't made a difference," he said.

There was clear and obvious evidence that E-Day was planned for PS5, but it was never released on Sony's console. Other industry experts said Microsoft purposefully sent E-Day out to die "for hearts and minds."

Additionally, Piscatella said Sharma's decision to remove new Call of Duty games from Game Pass was another loser of a decision. He said the data he's seeing shows that the Call of Duty franchise "lost a ton of engagement" due to Modern Warfare 4 being stripped out of Game Pass.

"And you got no benefit. It’s really hard to find any signs of positivity or hope on that platform right now," he said.

Piscatella went on to say that the efforts Microsoft is undertaking are for "Twitter likes" from hardcore fans. "But other than that, in terms of actual results, I'm not seeing anything right now," he said.

Sharma's turnaround plan for Xbox was never expected to yield immediate results--she only took the job in February and she inherited numerous foundational problems. In a memo to staff seen by CNBC, Sharma said she's taking a "long-term" view to help turn things around, and that includes pushing every studio to return to growth for players and revenue by the end of the fiscal year ending June 2027. Beyond games, Sharma has established a unit called XP, which will expand Xbox's games across film, TV, consumer products, sponsorships, and live experiences, as well as new initiatives in China.

Also in the memo, Sharma said she will push her teams to help Xbox get back in line with rivals Sony and Nintendo by 2027 in terms of profit margins, and then beat them by mid-2030. For comparison, Xbox currently reports about a 3% internal margin, which compares to 9.9% for PlayStation and 16% for Nintendo, according to CNBC.

A 3% profit margin means that for every $100 that Xbox brings in, it spent $97 to do so and keeps $3. A higher profit margin is better, and that's what Sharma is pushing for.

#3693. This Amazon Basics Power Bank Is 67% Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Woot has dropped the price of the Amazon Basics 20,000mAh portable charger in black to $12.99 from $38.99, making it considerably cheaper than the $34.85 the same model currently costs elsewhere. You also get free standard shipping if you’re a Prime member (while everyone else pays $6), but keep in mind Woot doesn't deliver to Alaska, Hawaii, P.O. boxes, or APO addresses.

For that price, you're getting a fairly substantial backup battery that measures 4.48 by 2.83 by 1.16 inches, making it compact enough to slip into a backpack or tote, although its 0.77-pound weight might make it a little bulky for a jacket pocket. The trade-off is a fairly generous 20,000mAh capacity that should be enough to recharge a typical smartphone several times, making it particularly useful for camping trips or long weekends when access to power outlets is limited. And since you're likely to have more than just your phone with you on those trips, the charger comes with two USB-C ports and one USB-A port, allowing you to charge up to three devices at once.

When used individually, either USB-C port can deliver up to 20W, enough to fast-charge many modern smartphones, while the USB-A port tops out at 12W, making it better suited to older devices and smaller accessories. The catch is that connecting two or three devices reduces the total output to 15W shared across the ports, so charging everything together will take longer than plugging in one device at a time. Both USB-C ports can also be used to recharge the power bank itself, which takes around 4.4 hours, and the box includes a 1-foot USB-C to USB-C cable for charging (it won’t transfer data).

All said, anyone hoping to charge a laptop will need a higher-wattage model, but for occasional travel, commuting, or keeping your phone running during a long day, the capacity and price make a reasonable combination.

The Marvel Cinematic Universe is constantly growing, thanks to exciting new projects arriving in theaters and streaming with a Disney+ subscription. Fans have a number of upcoming Marvel movies to look forward to, but the hype around Avengers: Doomsday is at a fever pitch. Folks are looking for any clues about what The Russo Brothers have up their sleeve, and there's a new reasons why fans (including me) think that Tom Holland's Spider-Man might end up having a surprise appearance.

What we know about Avengers: Doomsday is very limited, which is why moviegoers have been filling in the blanks with rumors and theories. The Doomsday cast list is a huge one, but Kevin Feige confirmed that more surprise appearances will be included as well. Merch for the movie has been rolling out, including a collaboration with Ray-Ban inspired by a number of heroes. Namely Captain America, Doctor Doom, Deadpool and (you guessed it) Spider-Man.

Some fans thought this might indicate that Deadpool is in Doomsday, and the concept of Spider-Man popping up seems even more likely. After all, Brand New Day and the next Avengers movie filmed at the time in Pinewood Studios in England. So it wouldn't take much more than some clever scheduling for Tom Holland to run over to the other end of the studio and shoot some footage as Peter Parker. Plus, he's one of the most popular characters in the entire shared universe.

The credits scene from Spider-Man: Brand New Day seemed to tease the web slinger popping up in either Doomsday or its sequel Secret Wars. Specifically the latter, as it showed a Spider-Man being spotted in space. Still, the Spidey Ray-Bans have other moviegoers crossing their fingers that Tom Holland's beloved hero will get to join the forthcoming battle again Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day became the highest grossing movie of all time upon its release, so it's clear that folks are invested in Tom Holland's ongoing tenure as the web swinger. As such, it seems like a no-brainer that The Russos and Marvel would want him included in the shared universe's next big crossover moments. We'll just have to see whether or not this theory ends up coming to fruition.

Deadpool & Wolverine also broke records at the box office, so it's possible that Ray-Ban was simply releasing new Marvel merch based on its most popular characters. Clearly the Marvel fandom is invested in the next Avengers movie, and it should be fascinating to see which characters actually appear.

All will be revealed when Avengers: Doomsday hits theaters on December 18th as part of the 2026 movie release list. Fingers crossed we see Spider-Man pop up throughout it mysterious runtime.

#3691. Xbox Wants To Be More Profitable Than PlayStation And Nintendo By 2030

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has an ambitious goal: not only to make Xbox more lucrative, but to surpass the profit margins of its biggest gaming rivals, Sony and Nintendo.

Speaking to CNBC, Sharma said Microsoft was working to achieve this goal by mid-2030 and had a variety of plans in place, from focusing on more exclusive titles to gaining more ground in the casual games market. "We will build long-term plans for our biggest franchises across film, television, consumer products, sponsorship, live experiences, and form new partnerships globally, including China," Sharma wrote in an Xbox memo, adding that the company will invest heavily in Minecraft and that revenue growth is expected to speed up in the 2028 and 2029 fiscal years.

"By Financial Year 2030, our ambition is to be halfway to our long-term daily-player goal with sustained double-digit growth in players and engagement and industry-leading margins," she wrote.

While Sharma aims to increase Xbox's player and revenue growth in the fiscal year ending June 2027, things don't look too good for the division right now. According to Circana tracking data, US Xbox Series hardware sales fell 27% year-over-year in September 2026--reaching a new all-time September low--and Sharma recently posted online that revenue had declined in the most recent financial quarter. Sharma added that "console sales remain constrained by supply," but she was vague on the specifics. At the same time, Xbox console prices rose again in August, making it more expensive than ever to buy one compared with its original launch price in November 2020.

Xbox has also gone through a brutal "reset" phase ever since Sharma took over, with over 1,600 jobs eliminated and several studios cut from the Xbox portfolio. If Microsoft wants to make Xbox more profitable than Sony and Nintendo, it could face an uphill battle, as Xbox recorded a 10% quarterly revenue decline. By comparison, CNBC reported that Sony reached a 9.9% operating margin from game and network services alone in its latest financial year, while Nintendo was close to 16% in its fiscal year.

Xbox's current strategy seems focused on more than just gaming, as the new XP division was unveiled earlier this month. Dedicated to movies, TV, and live events, it follows several recent multimedia project announcements, including the third season of the Fallout TV series, a Call of Duty movie, a Diablo animated series, and a Minecraft theme park opening in 2027.

#3689. WoW: Forever Controller Support Is A First Step To Playing The MMO On “Whatever You Want”

World of Warcraft: Forever will launch with full controller support, a first for the various versions of Blizzard's longrunning PC-exclusive MMORPG. According to Blizzard, the option to play on controller is the "first leg of a journey" to make WoW playable "on whatever you want." 

Speaking to GamesRadar, WoW executive producer and vice president Holly Longdale said Blizzard's goal is to eventually have WoW playable "wherever you want, and, at some point, on whatever you want."

The first step on that road, however, is ensuring controller support works really well. Blizzard is using the launch of Forever on November 4, the latest version of its MMO that reimagines the game's classic world and gameplay with new content and features, as a starting point.

"Looking at where things are going when we hear about Project Helix [the codename for Xbox's next console], et cetera, I think platforms will be a bit more ubiquitous," Longdale said. 

She continued: "I think just doing some of the work we're doing on gamepad [support] is going to give players a lot of flexibility that I think goes beyond consoles."

Having gone hands-on with Forever's controller support during BlizzCon 2026, I can say it works surprisingly well for a game that has been played almost exclusively with mouse and keyboard for 22 years. While modern WoW has added some barebones controller options in recent years, Forever's implementation is far superior, working seamlessly without the need for player-made addons like ConsolePort to make it usable. 

You have a surprisingly number of keybinds available at your fingertips (28, to be exact), making combat and interacting with quest NPCs a breeze. Inventory management and navigating menus is a little more cumbersome, but it does feel like a decent tradeoff for being able to play on a controller or a handheld, like the Xbox ROG Ally X. 

When WoW might be playable on something other than a PC remains to be seen, though Blizzard has made clear that if it were making a console version, it wouldn't exactly be a secret. 

But that doesn't mean WoW on consoles is still years away. Xbox's next console, Project Helix, is rumored to be a hybrid device capable of playing console and PC games, meaning WoW would likely be playable on it. According to a recent report, Project Helix is aiming for a 2028 release, may include a handheld component, and could possibly cost between $1,200 and $1,800 if Microsoft doesn't subsidize it.

In the meantime, Blizzard is plenty busy getting ready for Forever's launch, including reworking racial abilities and making improvements to the game's divisive layering system. If you bought the MMO's new optional playable race, the Skyborne, you can technically make your WoW: Forever character right now ahead of launch day. WoW: Forever launches November 4.
