#3665. Unpacking Nicki Minaj’s MAGA Style Evolution

This is the October 28, 2026 edition of Fit Check, your front row seat to the power players, peacocks, and deep pockets of fashion—and how they influence the rest of the world.

Pieter Mulier’s Versace debut will be marked with a couture show and the runway revival of Atelier Versace in January, and Bottega Veneta is back on Instagram for the first time since 2021—pouring one out to the fan accounts that had been enjoying their window of opportunity. Otherwise, the fashion news cycle has taken a break so far this week, so I’ve turned my attention to the midterm elections. Below, find missives on Nicki Minaj’s Gucci skirt suit by Demna—which was not provided to her by the brand—and the old style trick the Dems have adopted to appeal to us common folk. Plus, I get into why people love to clown Drake for his outfits. (For the record, I thought his Hermès by Martin Margiela fringed cape was fabulous.)

I wrote this edition of Fit Check wearing a sequined ghost costume (a ghost writer, get it?). It was my attempt at finding the right mindset to unpack what the internet has dubbed “gay Halloween,” for which I enlisted some of my fellow friends of Dorothy, and other experts, to help explain the formerly niche, now very viral internet phenomenon.

Mentioned in this issue: Jon Ossoff, Ralph Lauren, Bailey Moon, Juliet Charlotte, Marc Jacobs, Ariana Grande, Jonathan Anderson smoking a cigarette by the Seine, the breakup Post-it from a 2003 episode of Sex and the City, and many more.

“These Dem men with their hiked sleeves are taking me out,” read a comment under a clip of Senator Jon Ossoff and Pete Buttigieg on TikTok. “So hot.”

Ossoff and Buttigieg are the latest notable adopters of what appears to be the Democratic sartorial strategy for the ongoing midterm elections: to roll up their sleeves, literally. In a stark contrast to the most visible men on the right, who are all properly suited up both on the Hill in Washington, DC, and out on the campaign trail, “Dem men,” including Barack Obama and Gavin Newsom, have all been sporting a more casual look while campaigning. Individually, there’s nothing particular about the look. Obama and Buttigieg are former government officials; they’re technically off duty. Ossoff seems to want to position himself as a man of the people, and Newsom is working on embodying the anti-Trump. And yet, when seen together, the Dem men seem to have all agreed in a group chat to look a bit more working-class. No meticulously tailored Ralph Lauren suits, just dudes at work.

“There is a certain formula for cultivating a relaxed, approachable image while campaigning, versus the more polished presentation that comes with actually holding office,” says stylist Bailey Moon, who consulted with Dr. Jill Biden and Joe Biden during their time at the White House and worked with Tim Walz on the campaign trail in 2024. “It’s amusing to me, the idea that exposing your forearms suddenly makes you a man of the people, but rolling up your sleeves has become a political and metaphorical shorthand for being hardworking, accessible, and ready to get it done,” he says.

So is there a Dem men ’fit-pic group chat? “I don’t think there’s a coordinated effort,” Moon says. “I do think that politicians respond to a certain visual vocabulary, and right now, in a bid to win back working-class voters, that vocabulary is less formal and more familiar.”

Politicians do, in fact, think about their clothes more than we might think. “The visual language is always considered, even when the clothing itself isn’t front and center,” Moon says. “The challenge is making that feel instinctive rather than rehearsed, which ultimately comes down to the principal (key player) and how they carry it.” Ossoff et al. may not be folding up their sleeve cuffs as a joint campaign effort, and they may not be doing so to invoke some thirst in the comments section, but they’re making choices.

Drake celebrated his 40th birthday in New York City last weekend wearing black leather pants, a black turtleneck, and a brown fringed cape that got everyone talking. The rapper became the punch line of the weekend online before his outerwear piece was revealed as being a design by Martin Margiela during his time at Hermès—an archival holy grail find that Drake’s stylist, Juliet Charlotte, sourced from Canadian vintage seller Alex Maxamenko. He was called “Pumpkin Spice Papi,” a nod to his nickname and Instagram handle, @champagnepapi. He was compared to the Real Housewives venturing to Aspen on a girls trip. He was described as a rich auntie, and, my favorite, as ready for “Christian-girl autumn.”

The jokes were admittedly quite funny, and as we get into the “gay Halloween” phenomenon below, actor and comedian Sima Sepehri has already turned the viral moment into her costume. Yet underneath the surface of this mostly good-spirited fun—and my apologies for being the fun police—lies a layer of homophobia and, yes, misogyny. Drake has long been a punch line in the music industry and within hip-hop. People online have mocked him for the decor of his home and suggested he’d had a BBL or was showing off fake abs. He’s been called a wuss, and, pardon my French, a pussy. Which is where the issues with his style becoming a punch line begin.

Most of the jokes around Drake’s style compare him to women—to white women and their keenness for the fall season, to rich reality TV stars, to family matriarchs, and more. It’s simply too easy to call Drake and his penchant for fashion “feminine” or “fruity,” as if most famous men today, from his fellow rappers to athletes and actors, didn’t share his same affection for fashion and style. In a way, it’s not that serious. (And how he wore the shawl did look like he belonged more at a ski chalet than in the city.) Except that it kind of is; we have somehow not been able to shake gay as a zinger, and that’s generally because, culturally, we still consider femininity—and therefore women—to be less than masculinity and manliness. Let Drake wear his shawl. You’ve paid for it with your streams.

President Donald Trump and Nicki Minaj at a campaign event in Michigan.

President Trump made headlines last week for his comments on Senator Jon Husted’s physique, particularly his rear end. But he wasn’t done. This week, Trump attempted to crack a joke about it. “By the way, I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before, Nicki Minaj,” the president said on Sunday at a Republican campaign rally in Michigan. “That’s hard to miss,” he said, before looking at the rapper and instructing her to “stand up!” Minaj did, and waved to the crowd and the president as if thanking him for the…uh, compliment.

Minaj has been a puzzling character to watch as she ventures deeper into the MAGA-sphere—she’s even been jokingly floated as a potential next White House press secretary. (Minaj held a mock interview about Trump aboard Air Force One, which was posted to X by White House communications director Steven Cheung with the caption, “Ladies and gentlemen, I think we may have found the new White House press secretary! @NICKIMINAJ.”)

On Sunday, the rapper was wearing a skirt suit by Gucci, retailing for about $4,000. Her look was finished with Pink Friday press-on nails, her own brand, and matching Gucci-logo pumps. In a way, the outfit is a departure from what one usually sees onstage at MAGA rallies, where luxury fashion—and particularly logos—rarely reign supreme unless coming from the first lady. Minaj, unlike other Trump acolytes, is often clad in on-trend designer clothes (when she joined President Trump at the Treasury Department Trump Accounts Summit in January of this year, she was wearing an Alaïa dress by Pieter Mulier), and while the idea of a prim skirt suit certainly suggested she was dressed for business, or at least for politics, the loud, allover monogram logo felt like a remnant of the musical superstar that was, or that remains somewhere underneath the surface.

As for what this means for Gucci, its clients likely won’t find the image of Minaj deterring—it’s not like the brand is underwriting Minaj’s appearance or the messaging around it. But perhaps the image of Minaj onstage will inspire the MAGA set to adopt Demna’s revamp of the house—some of the caricatural archetypes in his most recent collection certainly leaned conservative. Funnily enough, Karlie Kloss, wife of Josh Kushner and sister-in-law to Jared, wore a similar pencil skirt at Demna’s first Gucci runway show.

#3664. New Assassin’s Creed Game Is Out Now, If You Don’t Mind Being Board

If you thought there wasn't going to be a new Assassin's Creed game this year, think again. It's not a video game, but Assassin's Creed: Animus is out today, turning the series into an adventure-style board game for 1-4 players.

A competitive game that pits players against each other as they explore distinct eras from the video games, Assassin's Creed: Animus features four protagonists to choose from in its standard edition: Eivor, Ezio, Altair, and Connor. The Collector's Edition, meanwhile, expands to 10 eras and features 16 protagonists, adding game characters like Edward Kenway, Jacob and Evie Frye, and Kassandra.

You and up to three of your friends (or you alone) work to complete objectives across these eras, taking down assassination targets in the way you see fit via "memory blocks." Whether you go in with your sword drawn or engage in a sneakier approach is up to you.

The standard version of Assassin's Creed: Animus is available to order now for $65, while the limited Collector's Edition costs $229. Alongside the extra characters and eras, this version comes with a storage box, acrylic tokens, a metal Piece of Eden, a cloth token bag, "special event cards," and an Animus Card Holder.

#3663. Lions Decline to Share More About Jack Campbell's Injury Out of 'Respect'

The Detroit Lions have declined to share any additional information on linebacker Jack Campbell’s potential neck injury as head coach Dan Campbell gave an update on his “recovery.”

“Jack Campbell continues to rest and recover at a local hospital,” the team said in a social media statement on Monday, November 2. “Preliminary indications are positive and out of respect for Jack and his family we will not share further information at this time.”

While the organization is prioritizing Jack’s family during this tough time, Lions coach Campbell, 50, briefly addressed the injury during a press conference that afternoon.

When asked by reporters on Monday whether he could share information on Jack’s health, Dan replied, “I can’t so I’m not going to. Next question.”

The head coach later shared that the team “does know what’s going on” and confirmed he has “updated the captains” following Jack’s scary collision during the Sunday, November 1, game against the Minnesota Vikings that seemed to leave the linebacker unable to move.

During Sunday’s game in Detroit, Michigan, Jack, 26, was involved in what appeared to be a relatively normal tackle against Vikings’ tight end T.J. Hockenson. After the collision, Jack was “immobilized” via a backboard and carted off the field.

Dan noted on Monday that “it’s about the recovery” now for Jack, adding that the player’s family is very “positive” about his future. (The team previously revealed Jack was being evaluated for a neck injury.)

He revealed that he’s spoken with Jack’s parents and wife Megan Campbell, adding that they are all in “good spirits.”

When it comes to Jack’s teammates, Dan confirmed that “a lot of people went over there, but not everybody got to see him” at the hospital because the doctors were “running some tests.”

Looking forward, the coach said that Jack’s absence will be felt by everyone in the organization.

“I don’t even know that I can put it into words — when you get voted captain that says a ton, especially with this group of guys,” he told reporters. “He earned every bit of that. He’s trustworthy, he’s dependable, he’d give the shirt off his back — he’s just all heart, man, all effort, and just an unbelievable person.”

Dan praised Jack as a man who is “down to earth” and “very genuine,” adding, “There’s not a man on this team that doesn’t respect Jack Campbell and care about him.”

Following Sunday’s scary tackle, some of Jack’s teammates have spoken out, including quarterback Jared Goff.

“Jack’s deal was definitely scary,” Goff, 32, said after the Lions victory over the Vikings on Sunday. “It just brings you back to reality for a moment that he’s a husband and a father. Scary. We’re praying for him and hope he’s going to be alright. If anyone is tough enough to get through something like that it’s going to be him.”

Vikings star Hockenson, 29, also reacted to the incident after the game, telling reporters, “I said this earlier, but prayers out to Jack Campbell, man, and his family. I was in on that play. I didn’t see what happened, but that’s an Iowa guy. I know Jack, and I just want to send good vibes to him and his family and his locker room.”

#3662. Everything You Should See Along With ‘You Can See Everything’

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

You Can See Everything, the new documentary about Theranos founder (and accomplished con artist) Elizabeth Holmes from filmmakers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, is breaking records (and brains). Not only is it raking it in at the box office in a way that few documentaries can manage, it’s also dominating the pop culture chat right now thanks to genre-defying techniques; a huge, rule-breaking twist (that I won't spoil); and its unrepentant and inexplicably mesmerizing subject.

While some might argue that you should head into this incredible film experience fresh, if you’re unfamiliar with any of the three major figures involved, you will benefit from a little prep work before you head in—and if you've already seen it, you're no doubt eager to dive even deeper into this truly remarkable (in every sense of the word) story. Here’s what you should watch, read, and listen to before or after You Can See Everything.

To put it simply: There’s a lot going on here. To ensure you can appreciate the film, you should make sure you know at least the basics about three things: Elizabeth Holmes (and why she’s infamous), and the work of both Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. Here’s the crash course.

The 2019 podcast The Dropout is one of the most efficient ways to get the background on Holmes and Theranos. In the style of a true crime podcast, this show from ABC and journalist Rebecca Jarvis offers a deep dive into Holmes and her crimes that will give you all the background you’ll need.

John Carreyrou is the journalist who broke the Holmes story wide open, and his award-winning book Bad Blood offers a more journalistic and less sensational investigation than other accounts, providing a close-up look at Holmes in her CEO persona—an alternately terrifying and charismatic person who comes across as a “character” Holmes is playing. The book will inform your viewing of the documentary in important ways.

While Nathan Fielder is getting most of the attention for You Can See Everything, co-director Lance Oppenheim brings his signature technique to the film—it wouldn’t be nearly as interesting without his visual sensibility and framing.

Oppenheim has helmed several notable films, as he’s made a name for himself as a brilliant documentarian over the last few years, but to get ready for You Can See Everything, check out Spermworld, his 2024 exploration of unregulated sperm donations (you read that right). The doc deals with people who are as reality-challenged, manipulative, and possibly delusional as Holmes, and it will prep you for his visual style of extreme close-ups and excessive coverage that seems almost impossible in a normal documentary setting. You can stream Spermworld on Hulu.

If you’re unfamiliar with Nathan Fielder’s work, you need to strap in, because he’s unlike any other comedian or documentarian you’ve ever encountered.

To get a sense of his style, start with Nathan for You, a comedy-documentary-reality TV hybrid in which Fielder—as a version of himself—tries to use his business experience to help struggling people and small businesses. Presented as totally sincere, Fielder’s ideas are nevertheless increasingly elaborate and, in a word, unhinged. This show will familiarize you with Fielder’s persona and approach, but if you only have time to cram one episode, check out the series finale, “Finding Frances.” It follows Fielder’s attempts to reunite one of his earlier clients with his long-lost love, and it is a nearly perfect encapsulation of his style and approach. You can stream Nathan for You on HBO Max, Hoopla or Paramount Plus, or rent it episode-by-episode on Prime Video.

You should also watch at least some of Fielder’s other series, The Rehearsal. Here, Fielder (again, portraying a version of himself) attempts to help people prepare for difficult conversations utilizing increasingly outlandish techniques and scenarios that spiral into comedic insanity, including building sets, hiring actors, and immersing himself and his subjects in an alternate reality of sorts—an approach that will prepare you for some of You Can See Everything’s swerves. If you don’t have time to watch the whole thing, just check out the first episode, “Orange Juice, No Pulp.” It’s a self-contained chapter and will give you the basics. You can stream The Rehearsal on Apple TV or HBO Max, or rent episodes on Prime Video.

Have more bandwidth before watching You Can See Everything, or want a deeper dive after the documentary has melted your brain? Here’s what else you can check out.

The companion podcast to Carreyrou’s book, Bad Blood: The Final Chapter, is well worth a listen. Hearing the journalist’s perspective about his investigation and work during and after Holmes’ trial offers additional insight into her personality and methods that will really resonate after watching her in Fielder and Oppenheim’s doc.

Once you’ve noodled on You Can See Everything for a moment, there are two more movies you should check out.

For more on Holmes’s specific grift and how she pulled it off, Alex Gibney’s excellent The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley is the way to go, especially if you didn’t follow the Theranos story closely at the time and your main visual guide to Holmes is the new documentary. Gibney’s film is more traditional, but offers a wealth of insight into Holmes and her bubble. You can stream The Inventor on HBO Max or rent it on Prime VIdeo.

If you more from co-director Lance Oppenheim, watch Some Kind of Heaven, his 2020 breakout documentary about The Villages retirement community in Florida. It’s the film that put Oppenheim on the map, and offers hints of the same detached observational style that makes You Can See Everything so arresting. You can stream Some Kind of Heaven on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Speaking of which, if you loved the visual style and “enhanced” reality of You Can See Everything and want to see more of that, catch the Robert Pattinson-starring Primetime, still in theaters. It’s Oppenheim's narrative film directorial debut, and combines his hyperstyled visual flair with thriller pacing and a narrative based on a true story.

The Curse, Fielder’s 2023 TV series, is his first work of fiction, and it offers some fascinating insights. It follows a newly married couple (played by Fielder and Emma Stone) who struggle to get an HGTV-style show off the ground as things get excruciatingly awkward (and, eventually, kind of surreal). After watching You Can See Everything, it will be interesting to see how Fielder views the power of editing, the ethics of reality TV, and working with a name actor to get the results that he wants. Plus, similarly to the film, The Curse swerves into a final act that will melt your brain. You can stream The Curse on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

You should also definitely watch The Dropout, the 2022 Hulu series starring Amanda Seyfried. It’s a well-made film, and Seyfried’s performance was rightly praised for capturing the weirdness of Holmes' public persona. You can stream The Dropout on Hulu.

#3661. Phantom Blade Zero’s Lead Voice Actor Was Seemingly Replaced At The Last Minute

There's a new voice behind the protagonist of Soul in Phantom Blade Zero, and it's none other than Sonic the Hedgehog--or his longtime voice actor, Roger Craig Smith, to be precise.

As spotted by Game Informer, Smith has stepped in to replace Jay Maksenuk (V in Once Human). You can still hear the latter in the various trailers for Phantom Blade Zero, and developer S-Game hasn't revealed why they brought Smith on as a last-minute replacement. Both actors have several video game credits, and as Game Informer noted, it sounds like Masenuk was replaced shortly after the game's review period began. Essentially, you won't be hearing Masenuk's voice, as the game launched earlier this week with Craig voicing the main character.

You're probably familiar with Craig's voice; in addition to Sonic and Batman, he's also voiced Ezio Auditore in several Assassin's Creed games, Daigo Dojima in Yakuza Kiwami 3, and Alden Dorne in Call of Duty: Black Ops 7. As a friendly reminder, set a hard limit on how much coffee Smith consumes if you're thinking of interviewing him.

Phantom Blade Zero has had a strong launch week so far, reaching over 730,000 concurrent players on Steam at the time of writing. If you're planning to play this weekend, check out our Phantom Blade Zero guides hub for dozens of walkthroughs, and if you're still on the fence, read our Phantom Blade Zero review to see if it's for you. Every Halloween, I think I've seen the year's best celebrity costume, and then somebody comes along and changes my mind. And while there's plenty keeping me entertained on the 2026 TV schedule, former Riverdale stars Madelaine Petsch and Camila Mendes just gave me a fictional show I'd absolutely watch. Petsch and Mendes spent Halloween dressed as Wilma Flintstone and Betty Rubble, respectively, and their ridiculously glamorous photo shoot has me wishing The Real Housewives of Bedrock were an actual series I could binge.

Petsch and Mendes shared the pictures in a joint Instagram post on Halloween, captioning them "The Real Housewives of Bedrock," complete with a bone emoji. Amber Asaly shot the photos, and they look like promotional stills for the most unhinged Bravo spinoff imaginable. Prehistoric sets, dramatic side-eyes, and enough attitude suggest somebody's about to get kicked out of the Bedrock country club. Seriously, take a look:

A post shared by Madelaine Petsch (@madelame)

Since Andy Cohen recently teased the possibility of more Real Housewives cities, I think somebody should put Bedrock on the list. Seriously, who’s Flintmobile’s stone log rollers do I gotta buff to get this thing greenlit?

Petsch nails Wilma's signature look: red curls piled high, a white one-shoulder dress with a jagged hem, and those enormous pearls. Mendes, meanwhile, makes a fantastic Betty in a blue dress, matching hair bow and sleek dark bob. They've kept the recognizable Flintstones details while giving everything a glossy, fashion-editorial makeover. I'd genuinely love to see the rest of their imaginary cast.

The photos are where the joke really takes off. In one, Betty leans over to whisper something into Wilma's ear, while Wilma looks appropriately scandalized. Another pic shows them posing with champagne glasses, and there are shots of the pair lounging among rocky scenery lifted from the cartoon. They even brought two little white dogs into the mix. I'm not sure what the dogs have to do with prehistoric suburbia, I suppose its hard to secure a tiny dino on short notice, so I’m glad the pups got an invite.

As much as I love the outfits, someone in the Instagram comments deserves a gold star for the funniest response to the entire shoot. User @herecomesjoey wrote:

RIP CW, you would’ve greenlit this show by Monday morning 😭👌🏽🔥😍

I've always had a soft spot for how the 1994 live-action Flintstones movie brought Bedrock to life, and these costumes have that same wonderfully ridiculous attention to detail. Only this time, Wilma and Betty look ready for a Bravo reunion special.

They don’t really produce their own original series anymore, but the CW is still on the air, and I laughed harder than I probably should have. Considering these two spent seven seasons on Riverdale, a show that got increasingly bizarre right up through its series finale, a CW-style Flintstones drama feels almost plausible. I can already hear the trailer voice-over: "In Bedrock, everybody has something to hide."

Of course, Petsch and Mendes have a history of taking Halloween costumes very seriously. Just last year, they dressed as Kim Possible and Shego, proving that transforming into beloved cartoon characters is becoming something of an annual tradition for these two. Before that, they joined fellow Riverdale alum Lili Reinhart to dress as the Gotham City Sirens for Halloween, after previously transforming into the Sanderson sisters from Hocus Pocus. This year's costume is a duo rather than a trio, but Reinhart still showed up in the comments with a perfect one-word endorsement: "Icons." I can't argue with her.

What really sells these pictures for me is how completely the actresses commit to the bit. They look ready to feud over a dinner-party seating chart carved into a stone tablet. Unfortunately, The Real Housewives of Bedrock isn't a real series. For now, it's an excellent Halloween photo shoot and another reminder that Petsch and Mendes know how to have fun together long after Riverdale ended. But if anybody wants to commission a pilot, I expect a reunion special hosted by a particularly exhausted Fred Flintstone.

Riverdale is streaming in its entirety with a Netflix subscription.

#3659. Nick Fuentes Opts Out of the 2026 Midterms, Unlike Fellow Livestreamer Hasan Piker

It was a little after 4:30 in the morning this past June when Andy O’Brian says he jolted awake to muffled banging on the door of his Los Angeles home. As he came face-to-face with close to a dozen LAPD officers, O’Brian had a hunch about who’d sent them and why. Moments later, one of the officers asked O’Brian: “Are you trying to kill a guy named Nick?”

The sheriffs that morning wouldn’t likely have known that the “Nick” in question was a reference to Nick Fuentes, the 28-year-old white supremacist streamer with some 1.2 million followers on X and one of the largest streaming audiences on the conservative news platform Rumble. They were even less likely to know that O’Brian, a longtime follower of Fuentes—or a “groyper,” as the faithful like to call themselves—says he was swatted because he recently questioned the streamer’s political tactics in a group chat.

“Usually the right fucks with people on the left,” O’Brian tells me on a phone call this past September. “But now the right is fucking with people on the right. Like, how do I explain to the cops that [they’d been called because] I’m not Nazi enough?”

In the world of anonymous online accounts that orbit Fuentes and share his radical “America First” political agenda, O’Brian was a central figure at just 21. Better known by his online handle, Chad Champion, he’d watched Fuentes’s streams from age 14, following him from platform to platform as he was continually banned. O’Brian started posting himself and grew into a far-right microcelebrity. He soon found himself welcomed into Fuentes’s small inner circle, the “groyper generals.”

But it’s not exactly clear where this so-called army is marching. With his increasingly massive following, Fuentes is positioned to be a kingmaker in conservative politics. He’s long spoken of remaking the Republican Party, and he seems to control a loyal voting bloc populated by one of the most coveted demographics in electoral politics right now: young men. But the culture O’Brian describes to me doesn’t sound like a vanguard of white nationalism or anything close to a political organizing operation like the Democratic Socialists of America. Rather, it sounds like most online communities: transient spaces anchored by a celebrity-like figurehead, in this case Fuentes, who, according to O’Brian, was more concerned with gaming and earning money from his nightly streams than true politicking. (A recent report in The Washington Post estimated he earned nearly $900,000 from “superchat” donations between early 2025 and March 2026.) Each night, after Fuentes’s shows on Rumble ended, O’Brian says a select few would be invited to play Fortnite with the influencer.

FAR FAR RIGHT Fuentes provided extreme-right counter-programming to Turning Point USA’s “The People’s Convention” in Detroit, Michigan, June 15, 2024.

The community is highly deferential to Fuentes, O’Brian says, eager to gain his favor by clipping and posting moments from his show or attacking his critics online. It can verge into sycophancy as groypers grow consumed with “glazing” the leader, O’Brian adds, to the point that Fuentes has come to resent his own movement. “He hates all of those people,” O’Brian says, referring to Fuentes, “and everyone in the inner circle hated me because I wasn’t dick-riding him.” (Fuentes, when reached for comment, says: “I hate some of them, definitely.”)

But the real problems started for Chad Champion when things moved from online spaces to electoral politics. Earlier this year, Fuentes chose to endorse James Fishback, a groyper-adjacent character who’d embarked on a longshot bid to become Florida’s next governor. Polling at the time had Fishback in the single to low double digits. It was a test for Fuentes’s real-world clout, and it didn’t go well: Fishback went on to win just 10% of the Republican primary vote this past August.

O’Brian voiced his dissent in a relatively small groyper group chat—“the Chadites”—and his heresy was swiftly leaked to the broader community. “Nick is burning his reputation over this dude,” read one of O’Brian’s texts about Fishback. Fuentes was furious, says O’Brian: “Nick told me I was creating ‘problems’ for him.” Soon after, according to O’Brian, Fuentes called him “disloyal” and targeted him in his Telegram chat as an “antifa” collaborator. (Fuentes denies ever targeting O’Brian or labeling him “antifa.”) Soon after came the swatting.

While O’Brian challenged Fuentes, others have been menaced by his followers simply for trying to build public-facing careers as members of his movement, which has no apparent goals in electoral politics as a seismic midterm election cycle plays out. Unlike a certain political influencer from the opposite side of the spectrum, Hasan Piker, who’s ventured out across the country to harness his influence in service of leftist challengers in Democratic primaries, Fuentes has made little effort to insert himself or his online movement into the physical places where the messy work of political organizing unfolds. Mostly, he seems content to sit on stream in his basement, often describing his viewers as “incels” and “retards” while he rakes in their donations.

It’s left many in this world wondering what exactly Fuentes is chasing: Mainstream approval? Power? Online clout? Dollars? Pure chaos? Does he simply feel the tide going out on Trumpism in his young audience? When I reached out to see if Fuentes would like to comment on this story, he first replied over text: “Groyper gossip? Boooooo.” A few hours later, however, Fuentes called me to offer a more thorough response.

It wasn’t always like this. For some young conservative men, Fuentes’s America First movement became a far-right oasis over the last decade, a taboo-shattering community connecting through irony-pilled memes and a desire to aggressively reshape the American right.

To most outsiders, Fuentes’s vision is a horrifying glimpse at the most mutated strain of conservatism on the political spectrum, one shot through with sneering expressions of white nationalism, antisemitism, race science, and misogyny. There’s cheering approval for Adolf Hitler and fascism in general. In the past year alone, Fuentes has suggested that women are “the number one political enemy in America,” that America needs a “dictator,” that Black people “cannot actually sound out words,” and that political asylum seekers are “illiterate peasants.” In October, Vice President JD Vance seemed to reference Fuentes’s long-running hostility toward his wife, Usha, an Indian American. “Theres this podcaster, who goes obsessively at me and my family,” he said. Fuentes responded by calling Vance an anti-gay slur. When it leaked that he’d sat down for dinner with Donald Trump and Kanye West in 2022, the reports created a massive scandal for the former-and-future president. And when Fuentes and a crew of manosphere influencers including Andrew Tate and Clavicular were captured singing along to West’s “Heil Hitler” at a South Beach nightclub this past January, it was the reactionary right on parade.

Fuentes was born in Chicagoland in 1998 and was something of a typical conservative growing up. But he proved a formidable communicator of extreme ideas while attending Boston University, where in 2017 he launched the show that would make his name: America First With Nicholas J. Fuentes. He attended the Unite the Right Rally in Charlottesville a few months later, dropped out of school soon after that, and became a professional purveyor of far-right vitriol.

YOUTH GROUP As an 18-year-old Boston University student, Fuentes showed up to a protest against Trump's travel ban on January 30, 2017.

He was eventually banned from Twitter (as well as YouTube, Twitch, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and Reddit), and his podcast was removed from Spotify for hate-speech violations. But his 2024 reinstatement on Elon Musk’s X has mainstreamed Fuentes’s words and clips. His post crudely mocking a liberal slogan to mark Trump’s victory in that year’s election—“Your body, my choice”—became one of the most viewed political posts of all time. Ever since he appeared on Tucker Carlson’s show last fall, Fuentes has become a kind of mythic figure in conservative circles, representing both the future of the right and all that has seemingly gone awry. This past week, HBO’s John Oliver devoted a large part of a segment to Fuentes’s growing reach. “Fuentes has been inching closer and closer to mainstream Republicans over the years,” he said.

But even as the young men with whom Fuentes has influence begin to sour on the president, discerning the streamer’s political goals is increasingly difficult. Over the course of Trump’s second term, Fuentes has mostly played the part of surly dissident, whipping up controversy between the right’s wobbly coalitions. He’s been openly antagonistic toward the Trump administration, and perhaps the most consistent message he’s conveyed to his followers this past year has been the abandonment of the GOP altogether, urging them to “vote Democrat.” For the Ohio governor’s race, one of the rare contests that Fuentes has directly commented on, he’s come out in support of a female Democratic candidate, Amy Acton, over her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, the Indian American entrepreneur who is a frequent target for the white nationalist right.

Meanwhile on X, many of Fuentes’s posts read like lusty-sounding fantasies about the coming onslaught awaiting Republicans this midterm election cycle. “I can’t wait for Republicans to get destroyed in the midterms and then everyone in the admin to be impeached,” reads one Fuentes post. His increasingly nihilistic streams often veer into political incoherence: He continues to engage in extreme racism and misogyny, said it would have been “better” for Kamala Harris to win in 2024 (to supposedly pave the way for “an American Hitler”), and now maintains the Trump administration is a “criminal enterprise.” His public statements have been laced with melancholy too. This spring he wrote in one post on X: “I’m getting really sick of politics honestly.”

For much of the past year, reports of doxxing, sustained harassment campaigns, and occasional swattings within Fuentes’s far-right faction have grown. These tactics once seemed reserved for the group’s perceived enemies on the outside, but they’ve increasingly become a way to punish or banish groypers deemed disloyal to Fuentes. Earlier this year, after CNN aired an interview with two men who self-identified as groypers, Fuentes brutally mocked the pair on stream—criticizing them for, among other things, their normie footwear. In the ensuing pile-on, both were savagely harassed across social media platforms, with groypers even calling for them to be doxxed.

Then there’s the more drastic case of Amy Dangerfield. A former “groypette” and content creator, Dangerfield earned the ire of Fuentes and his generals for the sin of attempting to organize a conference of America First politicians and streamers this past May. Her goal, she claimed at the time, was to bring Fuentes’s political agenda into the real world, and she invited a coalition of right- and left-leaning politicians and influencers to hash out the idea of an “America First” political agenda. The attempt backfired massively. On his Telegram channel, Fuentes claimed that Dangerfield was trying to subvert him, and referred to her as “Amy Dangerslut.”

PROTAGONIST Fuentes has been accused of running a cult of personality without real political goals.

The claim led to a torrent of stomach-churning abuse and harassment directed at Dangerfield and her husband. A story in The Washington Post described how a flood of torture images and doctored content were unleased against the former Fuentes devotee, all because she hadn’t received his blessing to stage a public event. Today, Dangerfield has largely stepped back from far-right politics and her once-promising streaming career.

For years, Fuentes has claimed that his primary objective is the slow takeover of the Republican Party. He often boasts that the groypers are “inside” the institutions of government, and recent reports in the media have traced how Fuentes’s ideas have permeated the young Republican cadre working in Congress and establishment think tanks such as the Heritage Foundation. Fuentes himself likes to brag about the fellow travelers he says are working within the Trump administration, and O’Brian tells me that he’s heard from groypers in DC that Fuentes has traveled there on occasion to meet with his young allies who work in the White House.

But many on the far right find this slow-burn strategy to be a fantasy—or cover for Fuentes’s unwillingness to take larger political risks. Some believe he actually wants to change lanes.

“I think that he saw that the market opened up following the assassination of Charlie Kirk, which is why he’s coming after everyone who is questioning that narrative,” Dangerfield says when I call her up to ask her thoughts. She’s referring to Fuentes’s clashes with Candace Owens over who killed Kirk and why. “I just think he wants to make his money and go mainstream.”

More sympathetic observers on the right think Fuentes’s disinterested approach to electoral politics is a deliberate choice. Aidan Thompson, who’s behind the widely read America First news platform, AF Post, tells me that Fuentes is holding back out of a sense of “responsibility” to his audience and a refusal to support a flawed GOP slate of candidates.

“I think Nick is tapping out because Trump and the party have just totally fucked him off,” Thompson says. “Like, why would you show up?”

When I eventually get Fuentes on the phone, he takes that tack. “I’ve been very open about why I’m not supporting Trump, and that’s because he started a war with Iran,” he says, claiming that many of his predictions about the second Trump presidency have ultimately come true: the war; a perceived failure to follow through on mass deportations; and that the administration is stocked with neoconservatives, America First’s internecine enemies on the right. “All of those things came to fruition,” Fuentes tells me.

He dismisses criticisms that he’s simply sitting out the midterms or trying to poison the GOP’s chances. “People say I’m just sour grapes over Trump or Peter Thiel,” he says, referencing reports that he pitched the latter for funding and failed. “But I’m very open about my problems with these people. It’s all ideological.” Fuentes goes on to explain his strategy is an attempt to correct a “generational mistake” by previous America First candidates like Pat Buchanan, whose followers ultimately lined up behind the Republican Party. Fuentes has instructed his followers to withhold their votes, estimating that this bloc could add up to some 3% of the general election vote. “We can exercise the veto, and I think that’s the source of our power,” he says.

As the midterms drag on with a sense of grinding doom for Republicans, all that might be too conceptual for a younger generation of conservatives hungry to see a far-right takeover of the party. Will Fuentes and his movement stay stuck on the internet, or can they break out? For her part, Dangerfield suggests the failed Fishback endorsement was evidence that Fuentes doesn’t have the “political pull he thinks he does,” while O’Brian is more blunt still: “He clearly can’t be the guy to take things to the next level.”

#3658. CoD: Modern Warfare To Cut Real-Life Korean Tragedy Segment After Backlash

Publisher Activision has responded to criticism over using a devastating tragedy in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, saying that the incident will be removed from the military shooter in a November 12 update.

The Seoul Halloween crowd crush occurred in October 2022 in Itaewon. Approximately 100,000 people gathered in a narrow alleyway in Seoul, resulting in 160 casualties as people were suffocated. This year marks the fourth anniversary of the tragedy, with bereaved families and community organizers gathering to remember the lives that were lost.

Modern Warfare 4 hit consoles and PC on October 23, and not long after its release, the game drew criticism from bereaved Korean families. In the opening cutscene to the game's campaign--which focuses on a fictional war between North and South Korea--Modern Warfare 4 depicts a chaotic scene where one person performs CPR on a downed individual, while bodies are either laid out on the streets or carried away on stretchers. Given the game's setting and the events on screen, the 10.29 Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association and the Citizens' Countermeasures Meeting--two organizations formed after the 2022 tragedy in Seoul--were "appalled" at the calamity's inclusion and demanded that Activision remove it from the game.

"Using such an incident as material for a game intended for entertainment purposes is itself highly inappropriate and a senseless act," the groups said, according to the BBC. "The Itaewon tragedy was a tragic disaster that produced hundreds of casualties, and citizens who participated in the rescue efforts or witnessed the event at the time continue to suffer from trauma. If the game developer has even a minimum level of courtesy and empathy toward the victims, they should promptly take corrective measures."

Activision has heard the call and plans to remove the depiction from Modern Warfare 4 when an update arrives on November 12. In responding to the criticism, Activision said it never intended to trivialize the disaster or make light of human suffering.

"In developing Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, we approached the subject matter with care and respect. The game’s opening cinematic utilises some real-world news coverage to establish the game’s fictional narrative," Activision said. "It is not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape or form."

#3657. 'Doomsday Mom' Lori Vallow Daybell Seeks New Trial in Killings of Her 2 Kids

Lori Vallow Daybell is requesting a new trial as she appeals her convictions in the killings of her two children and for conspiring to kill her husband’s former wife.

Vallow Daybell’s attorney appeared before the Idaho Supreme Court on Monday, November 2, when the court heard an appeal to overturn her convictions, per KSL-TV.

In 2023, Vallow Daybell, who has doomsday religious beliefs, was convicted of killing her son, 7-year-old Joshua “JJ” Vallow, and 16-year-old daughter, Tylee Ryan, according to the Associated Press. Following the children’s disappearances in 2019, their bodies were found buried on an Idaho property belonging to her then-new husband, Chad Daybell.

Lori was also found guilty of conspiring to kill Chad’s first wife, Tammy Daybell, in connection with her death.

Lori ultimately received three life sentences in Idaho for the deaths of Joshua, Tylee and Tammy, per the Associated Press. Chad was sentenced to death in connection with the murders.

While Chad was on trial, Lori’s niece testified Lori and Chad were a part of a “doomsday cult,” per ABC affiliate KTVX.

Lori was separately handed two life sentences in Arizona in 2025 after she was convicted of a conspiracy to kill her ex-husband, Charles Vallow, and her niece’s husband, KSL-TV reported. Charles was fatally shot in Lori’s home while the niece’s husband survived a separate shooting.

Lori’s attorney has contended in Lori’s appeal heard by the Idaho Supreme Court that she was denied a speedy trial and deprived of her right to retain counsel of her choosing, per the Associated Press. The lawyer also argued that a lower court shouldn’t have allowed Idaho jurors to hear information on the separate Arizona shootings against Charles and her niece’s husband, Brandon Boudreaux, who survived after a shot missed him.

Lori’s brother, Alex Cox, fatally shot Charles in July 2019 after Charles had filed to divorce Lori, the outlet reported. Cox claimed he killed Charles in self-defense.

Prosecutors argued Lori plotted with her brother to kill Charles to obtain Charles’ life insurance policy money when she had been dating Chad. Cox, who was also accused of opening fire on Boudreaux, has since died due to a blood clot.

During Lori’s appeal, judges asked whether overturning her verdict could result in her facing the death penalty in the event of a retrial, per NewsNation.

The court hasn’t reached a final decision on the appeal.

#3655. EA Just Shelved A Mysterious Sims Project—That Could Be Good News For Players

It's been another rough year for video games, with countless studio closures, staff layoffs, and projects that barely managed to even get off the ground before they were unceremoniously cut short. But things are feeling especially grim after EA trotted out two beloved franchises--Mass Effect and Dragon Age--for what amounted to a public execution via the announcement that BioWare has been shuttered. 

This was especially painful for Mass Effect players, who were looking forward to the upcoming Mass Effect 5, which we now know was tentatively titled Mass Effect: Universe. But it's not just BioWare fans who are upset at the moment. Fans of EA's other properties are growing increasingly concerned about the future of those franchises, if any future is planned for them at all. My colleague Levi Winslow recently wrote about their concerns for the Skate franchise in the wake of layoffs at its development studio. Meanwhile, I'm quite worried about the fate of The Sims.

In the same breath it announced the end of BioWare, EA also reaffirmed its commitment to Apex Legends, Skate, and The Sims franchises. But everyone knows that when it comes to profits, EA's sports titles outrun its other IPs by a country mile. If EA is willing to pull the plug on legacy franchises like Mass Effect and Dragon Age, where does that leave its other franchises, like The Sims 4?

According to EA, Sims fans need not worry, as the company is committed to "focusing on the long-term potential of The Sims." Apparently, focusing on that long-term potential involves shelving a project The Sims team has been working on for years: Project Rene, AKA Project Lotus, AKA the nebulous next entry in The Sims franchise, which appears to be some kind of weird Sims MMO mobile game thing. Instead, EA will be focusing on Project Evergreen, which is rumored to be a sort of remaster of The Sims 4, with all (or most) DLC packs included, and recurring bugs squashed.

"We're supporting this franchise by pausing work on one of the next titles in this franchise" doesn't exactly inspire confidence, especially after the nonchalance with which EA just killed two other beloved game franchises. But I think this actually might be the right move. 

It's been a bumpy couple of years for The Sims, and many players aren't particularly enthused about Project Rene/Lotus, as it seems to be once again trying to recreate The Sims Online, something EA has tried to rebuild over and over. In fact, much of the reason The Sims 4 launched in such awful shape was due to the fact that it was initially meant to be an MMO-style game that could run on mobile devices. Less than a year before launch, EA pivoted to a more traditional Sims game--but by then, so much of the game had been built with online play and mobile devices in mind that it was too late to turn back. Despite releasing over 100 DLC packs and embarking on a concentrated campaign to squash the game's many, many, many bugs, longtime Sims players are still frustrated with the state of The Sims 4, often pointing out the numerous ways it pales in comparison to its predecessor, The Sims 3. 

The Sims 4 is officially "done" in that there are no plans to release any more expansion packs for the game. When it comes to the future of the franchise, most players don't want the next Sims title to be yet another attempt at shoehorning online and/or mobile gameplay into a game that is, at its core, all about building and playing with digital dolls in their digital dollhouses. So EA's decision to hit pause on Project Rene/Lotus's development isn't something I find especially heartbreaking. In fact, I think it's the first truly wise decision EA's made regarding the franchise in a long time, provided EA actually plans to support Project Evergreen long-term (which the name Evergreen would suggest).

Sims 4 players don't want Project Rene, but they do want either The Sims 5 or a complete, playable version of The Sims 4--ideally one that doesn't require the purchase of $1,600 in DLC packs to feel "finished." Hitting pause on its weird, experimental Sims projects in favor of attempting to preserve The Sims 4 in a stable, playable, "evergreen" state is arguably the best decision EA could make, given the current state of both EA and The Sims franchise. Pouring resources into a concept that has failed before (online MMO-style Sims gameplay) rather than a tried-and-true formula (a digital dollhouse) would only harm the franchise at this point.

Of course, there's no telling what kind of shape Project Evergreen will launch in, assuming it does successfully make it to launch. It sounds like the Evergreen devs have a deadline to hit--hence the reshuffling of resources away from Rene/Lotus--but even with the increase in development resources, there's no guarantee Evergreen will be a massive hit with players.

Provided the rest of development does go smoothly and Evergreen is indeed well-received by players, it may still fall short of EA's goals when it comes to profits. EA has spent the last decade doing everything possible to monetize the living hell out of The Sims 4, a game that--unlike EA's lucrative sports catalog--is largely intended to be a solitary gaming experience that doesn't require online play. Back in the olden days of The Sims 1, 2, and 3, players would purchase the base game, a few expansion packs, and maybe a couple of "stuff packs" for extra decor options, but that was all one really needed to enjoy the game. 

The Sims 4, however, introduced an era of seemingly endless DLC: expansion packs, game packs, stuff packs, kits--there are over 100 of them, ranging in cost from $40 to $5, and totaling around $1,600 if purchased individually outside of sales and bundles. In addition to the constant stream of DLC releases, EA has in recent years implemented daily login rewards, various events and challenges, and even a paid mod store nobody asked for--all in the hopes of getting players to spend more time and money on The Sims 4. For a while there, I half-expected EA to implement a Sims 4 battle pass.

There's no telling what sort of irritating monetization tactics we'll see in Project Evergreen, but at the very least, Evergreen sounds like an attempt to try and maintain the series' roots, rather than continue chasing the mobile MMO Roblox-like direction Project Lotus seemed to be taking. Even better, Evergreen may turn out to be the game Sims players have been aching for since The Sims 4 launched to middling reviews back in 2014: a game that isn't fundamentally broken and lacking in content.

The real question is if Evergreen will be successful enough to keep The Sims franchise alive. Given that EA's new owners were happy to kill off what was shaping up to be a potentially great Mass Effect game, it's not hard to imagine a world where the Grim Reaper inevitably comes for The Sims, regardless of whether players love or hate Project Evergreen. After all, feelings don't generate dollar signs, and EA's new owners have made one thing abundantly clear: killing off an iconic franchise is "worth it" if it saves EA a few Simoleons.

#3654. Inside Gatcombe Park, Princess Anne’s Beloved 730-Acre Country Estate

On any given day at Gatcombe Park, Princess Anne’s sprawling 730-acre privately owned estate in Gloucestershire, one might spy the 76-year-old checking in on her prized Highland cows, a scarf tied firmly over her famous bouffant. At the estate’s cutting-edge stables, her daughter, Zara Tindall, may be riding with her daughter and nieces, coaching them as they jump through courses designed by her father Mark Phillips. Meanwhile, Zara’s husband, rugby star Mike Tindall, may be playing beer pong in the “party barn” with his brother-in-law Peter Phillips, while Princess Anne’s husband Sir Timothy Laurence watches rugby in the cozy, cluttered parlor of the estate’s main Georgian mansion.

The scene is that of an idyllic country estate, a beloved family home that is also a working farm. It may also serve as an example to Prince Harry and Meghan Markle as they search for their own private estate in the British countryside. “Being able to take on a place like this—for me, I’ve got to make it work,” Princess Anne once said. “This is not something that comes free, this has got to pay its way, otherwise I can’t stay here."

Since the ’70s, Gatcombe Park has been Princess Anne’s place of refuge from endless royal duties, a place to live the country life she loves. “Every year, month and day, I realise how fortunate and privileged I am to have grown up and spent most of my life in the countryside,” she told Country Life in 2020. “It’s not only the space, appreciating the seasons, the wildlife, the plant life, the arable crops and the livestock, but, most importantly, it’s the people who live and work there and understand the complexity of their environment.”

The estate was the perfect wedding present from the late Queen Elizabeth to her athletic, no-nonsense daughter and her first husband, Mark Phillips. The two Olympic equestrians first met at a party in 1968, although the meeting was not auspicious. “We had to be told that we’d met in 1968 before we remembered,” Anne recalled.

Zara Phillips riding her horse Toytown at Gatcombe Horse Trials, with Princess Anne and Tim Laurence, September 16, 2001.

They later reconnected and found they shared many things, including an obsession with nature, country life, and the world of elite equestrian competitions. “Anne couldn’t marry her horse, so she’s marrying Mark,” the then Prince Charles reportedly joked about his future brother-in-law. Princess Anne approached their upcoming wedding with the same stoicism she did everything. When asked if their relationship could withstand the pressure of publicity and public duties, the Princess was blunt. “Can? It’s got to, hasn’t it.”

The two were married on November 14, 1973, in a lavish ceremony at Westminster Abbey. From the start, Phillips, an active captain in 1st The Queen’s Dragoon Guards, proved to be cut from a different cloth. He refused all the Queen’s offers of titles and was not popular with some royals and their courtiers, with the protective Prince Charles reportedly nicknaming him “fog,” because he was “so thick, according to Kitty Kelley’s The Royals.” British journalist Auberon Waugh (the eldest son of novelist Evelyn Waugh) was even more brutal. He unkindly described him as “Princess Anne’s grinning, speechless husband, who, if you whistle at him, wets himself.”

The entrance hall with a stone floor and decorative pillars, June 1976.

In spite of naysayers, the couple forged ahead and began searching for the perfect country estate (“I’ve never been a city girl,” Anne noted). In 1976, former Home Secretary Lord Rab Butler, suggested the couple check out Gatcombe Estate, his family home outside of the village of Minchinhampton.

The estate featured over 700 acres of woods and cultivated farmland, stables, a fine herd of Hereford-Friesian cattle and a trout lake, “netting an income of between 14,000 and 18,000 pounds a year.” The five-bedroom neoclassical main house, built with Cotswold stone, was originally built in 1774. In 1820, the famous economist Davis Ricardo had the house redesigned. The exterior was covered in roses and wisteria, and the couple were instantly smitten. The interior was not as picturesque, with one friend describing it as “rather dreary, in some disrepair, with suspicions of dry rot.”

But the couple loved it. “We stood on the front steps and looked out at the view; it was quiet, it was secluded, it was peaceful with woods down each side of a long valley,” Phillips recalled. “I thought to myself—well, whatever is inside, we can change, given time. But this we can never change. This is just what we have been looking for.”

Peter Phillips, age 9, on horseback at Gatcombe Park, July 28, 1987.

A week later, Princess Anne took Queen Elizabeth to view the property. In June 1976, it was announced the Queen had purchased the home for the couple for a reported 500,000 to 750,000 pounds at the time. Workers on the estate suggested to reporters that Anne could help on a tractor. “Since the Princess can drive a tank, why not?” one quipped.

There was immediate backlash to the private purchase. “When members of the Labour Party government heard that the Queen was buying her daughter and son-in-law the farm and woodland property at such a price, left-wing members called for the introduction of a wealth tax,” the Australian Woman’s Weekly reported. “They pointed out that last year Parliament voted the royal family an extra $600,000 to help it pay its bills.”

MP Willie Hamilton took it a step further. “They’re gold-plated parasites. The lot of them. All parasites.”

For their part, the palace was tight-lipped, claiming the purchase was “an absolutely private matter.” Lord Butler also scoffed at the reported price, claiming it was not nearly as high.

Ignoring the noise, the couple began working to improve their new estate, insisting they would pay their own way. “People never believe me when I say that we’re just like any other young married couple with a mortgage,” Phillips said. Princess Anne did indeed drive a tractor, and Prince Andrew and Prince Edward were said to come down to help during harvest season. While his wife stayed at her apartment working in Buckingham Palace in London during the week, Phillips worked tirelessly on the farm, “so tired that I fell asleep in front of the television.”

Making good on their dream to turn Gatcombe into an A+ equestrian facility, the couple in 1983 hosted the inaugural Gatcombe Park Festival of British Eventing. The event became a mainstay on the elite equestrian calendar. Held every August, it featured Olympians competing in cross-county (courses often designed by Phillips), jumping and dressage events. Thousands attended the televised program each year, and many more visited at the annual craft fairs and the Gatcombe Food Festival.

Princess Anne with her bull terrier dogs at the British Horse Trials Championships, August 31, 1996.

Phillips found many ways to monetize the estate, even turning brushwood cleared from the courses into paintbrushes. Meanwhile, the couple raised their children Peter and Zara at Gatcombe, where life revolved around horses. “One enjoys riding, but when you get back there’s still half a day’s work to do just to keep the darn things on four legs,” Anne noted, per The Princess Royal by Helen Cathcart. “You have time for nothing else.”

Tindall has noted that she had an “amazing” country childhood on the estate, far from the hustle and bustle of royal life. “It was a great place to grow up around horses, looking after animals—the respect and partnership that you have to build with the animals, it teaches you so much you know growing up and as a kid,” she said.

But this didn’t mean that growing up on the farm wasn’t hard work. The Phillips children (whose parents declined for them to have titles) were expected to carry their weight. “We had to do everything with them,” Zara recalled. “We had to clean our tack. We had to muck them out.”

Zara, who eventually became an Olympic rider herself, recalled that her parents had very different ways of training. “Mum’s very relaxed. She’s like, Just, you know, just do what you do, whereas my father’s like, More of this, more of that, she said. “My father was quite critical... Very rarely you would get a, Yeah, that was good, out of him. So it was always striving to try and get that comment. He was a tough coach.”

There was also tension inside the home. Both Princess Anne and Phillips were unfaithful (Phillips even had a daughter, Felicity, with a New Zealand woman in 1985) and in 1989 they separated. But Phillips did not go far, moving to Aston Farm on the estate and continuing to run Gatcombe’s events (he finally left Aston Farm in 2013). Princess Anne stayed in the main house with her new husband, Sir Timothy Laurence, who she married in 1992.

According to those who have visited the main house, life there is surprisingly “unroyal” and laid-back, filled with bric-a-brac and cozy, worn decor. “Journalists and biographers who visit Gatcombe for the first time are still struck by the informality of the place,” Anne’s biographer Nicholas Courtney told Glocester Live. Gatcombe Park has become a true family compound, with Peter Phillips and his family reportedly having a cottage there. Zara and Mike Tindall have raised their children at Aston Farm since 2013.

Running the estate has also become a family affair. Peter Phillips helped organize the annual Gatcombe Park Festival of British Eventing in later years. Princess Anne would present trophies and Zara would compete, as photographers took pictures of Anne’s grandchildren frolicking.

Zara Phillips, Mia Tindall, and Princess Anne at the Whatley Manor Horse Trials, Gatcombe Park, September 8, 2017.

Farming operations have also continued, a practice Anne clearly relishes. “I have lived at Gatcombe for more than 42 years,” Anne wrote in Country Life in 2020. “We were not looking for a farm, but it has been a real privilege to try to work with what we have. Ours is an organic, extensive grass enterprise, usually complicated by running the horse-trial championships in early August. The woodland is a real mix of trees—mostly beeches, but huge numbers of ash of all ages. Who knows how many will survive, but I feel the naturally selected mix could be an important part of the answer.”

That same year, the official royal website also noted the extensive livestock on the property that included 230 Wiltshire Horn sheep, 14 White Park cows, 6 Highland cows, and 2 Gloucester Old Spot sows. There is also a prized herd of rare Suffolk Punch horses, which Anne is passionate about saving. The estate also includes a kitted out party barn, which includes catering facilities, large screens and bar/lounge areas.

The last few years have been eventful, in both good and bad ways. In 2021, Zara gave birth to her third child, Lucas, on the bathroom floor at Aston Farm. In 2023, the estate hosted their last Eventing Festival, citing rising costs and COVID as the reason.

“The horse trials at Gatcombe and more recently the Festival of British Eventing have been a major part of my life for over 40 years when The Princess Royal and I first had the dream,” Mark Phillips said in a statement at the time. “It’s truly a great sadness that the original model and indeed the sport has changed so much. Since COVID, costs, particularly insurance, have risen so much that the numbers no longer add up. It is an end of an era, the next 40 years of the sport will be different, let’s hope it can be equally special.”

In 2024, Princess Anne was reportedly injured by a horse on the property, which resulted in her being hospitalized for a concussion. But there was happier news in June of 2026, when Peter Phillips and his new wife Harriet Sperling reportedly celebrated their wedding reception at the party barn.

Although Princess Anne still continues with her punishing schedule of official engagements, staying in her London apartment in St. James Palace when she must, it is clear her heart lies at Gatcombe Park, surrounded by her loved ones, beloved animals and the crisp country air. “It’s very normal; there isn’t any standing on ceremony, and she’s the only one with a title,” royal historian Robert Hardman told Hello!. “She’s a very good grandmother. She’s hands-on, but like all grandchildren, I think they can get away with things. She dotes on them.”

In fact, the normally tight-lipped Anne has said so herself. “It’s really nice to come back and just be yourself in an area like this.” Former royal courtier Ailsa Anderson agrees. “Gatcombe is her bolthole, where she is not the Princess Royal—she is Anne.”

#3653. Gang Of Dragon Won’t Be The First Game From Nagoshi Studio. It Won’t Be Any Game At All

Nagoshi Studio, the studio formed by Yakuza creator Toshiro Nagoshi at NetEase, has been shut down before it even released its first game. According to Gematsu, shareholders officially dissolved the developer on October 31 via a resolution later published in the Japanese government gazette Kanpo.

Under Nagoshi, the studio worked on Gang of Dragon, a new game that looked similar to the veteran developer's work on Sega's Yakuza and Like a Dragon series at Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio. Work on the game continued over the years, and a trailer was shown at The Game Awards last year, but in March, reports said NetEase had pulled its funding for the project. The official Gang of Dragon YouTube channel also went down for a brief time in April, and in May, the game's website was whacked.

So why did the studio shut down? Exact details on the reasoning behind its closure haven't been revealed yet, but in March, Bloomberg reported that Nagoshi was seeking another $44 million to get Gang of Dragon across the finish line, a figure NetEase may have decided wasn't worth investing in further.

Meanwhile, Nagoshi's former home, RGG Studio, has released multiple games since he left. Nagoshi's final credits with Sega were for Lost Judgment, Super Monkey Ball Banana Mania, and Virtua Fighter 5: Ultimate Showdown; since then, RGG Studio has released five games in the Yakuza/Like a Dragon franchise. These include prequels, sequels, and remakes: Like a Dragon: Ishin, Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name, Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth, Gaiden: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii, and Yakuza Kiwami 3 & Dark Ties.

Next year will see the launch of Stranger Than Heaven, described as a distant prequel to Like a Dragon that spans 50 years.

The new reboot of Baywatch is just a couple of months away. We won’t see it on the 2026 TV schedule, but in the depths of the cold winter in January, we’ll be headed back to the beach on Fox. Two stars of the new version, Stephen Amell and Brooks Nader, recently spoke about some of the stars of the original Baywatch possibly returning in the reboot (other than the couple of former lifeguards who have been announced), and that led Nader to talk about some advice she got from Carmen Electra.

While talking to a gaggle of reporters hyping up the show, Nadar told them (via Deadline):

I spoke to Carmen Electra, and she said…. She just was like, ‘Oh my gosh, this is gonna be great.’ All she said about the series is how much hard work you have to actually put into it and how physically taxing it is on your body. And I heard at the beginning of filming, and I was like, ‘Eh, [I] got this.’ She was totally right in every way possible.

This isn’t the first time that Electra has given this advice to the new cast, telling E! back in June the same thing. It also seems as though the cast has gotten the message, as Amell has talked about all the prep he’s putting in to deal with the long, shirtless days and hours in the Pacific Ocean. Nadar has also joked about how her whole life is now “running in slow motion” since landing the gig.

Though Amell and Nadar were a little coy in their answer about returning stars, only hinting that some big names may show up, they definitely left the door open. Electra, of course, was one of the biggest stars during Baywatch’s original run in the 1990s. Whether she is going to return or not isn’t unknown. She’s said in the past that she is interested in returning (and even donned the old red suit earlier this year), provided she doesn’t have to shoot anything in the water.

Elektra has talked a lot about the new show and how hard it’ll be to recapture the magic of the original show. She knows it’ll be hard to replace icons like Yasmin Bleeth and Pamela Anderson, for example. Nadar isn’t taking the responsibility lightly, though, even perfecting her mouth-to-mouth for the show.

Whether the new show can recapture whatever lightning in a bottle the OG show had remains to be seen, but from all the interviews, it seems the cast knows exactly what the goal is, and they are really going for it.

#3651. MLB Free Agent Kike Hernandez Shares Glimpse Into His Life as a Dad

While becoming a World Series champion with the Los Angeles Dodgers was a dream come true, Kiké Hernández’s greatest title is “dad.”

“I’m definitely the fun dad. I can be firm, but I don’t know how necessarily strict I am because I’m not the most strict person in the world,” Kiké, 35, exclusively shared with Us while teaming up with Warner Bros. for a new initiative celebrating the iconic DC Super-Villains. “But I have an amazing support system in my wife [Mariana P. Vicente Hernández].”

He continued, “My wife is amazing. She’s an unbelievable mom, and I couldn’t have picked a better life partner for me. My wife’s got everything covered. That allows me to be myself with my kids and just be the same person and have fun with them.”

After another successful season with the Los Angeles Dodgers — who ultimately lost to the Milwaukee Brewers in the 2026 National League Championship Series in October — Kiké is now savoring quality time with daughter Penélope, 5, and son Santiago, 8 months, during the off-season.

While Kiké joked that his son is so young that he can only “carry him, rock him and feed him,” it’s a different story with his daughter.

“Going on walks with my daughter is probably one of the most fun things that I can think of. We tend to have pretty fun conversations,” he shared with Us. “I always tell my daughter, ‘Holding your hand is my absolute favorite thing in the world,’ and hopefully she might feel the same way.”

During Halloween weekend, Kiké and Mariana joined their daughter in dressing up as characters from Suicide Squad.

“I’ve dressed up as a Joker in the past for Halloween,” Kiké shared. “My wife has dressed up as my Harley Quinn, so obviously, the Joker is the house favorite. Honestly, my favorite movie of all time is The Dark Knight. I think Christian Bale and Heath Ledger made a pretty iconic movie.”

With another season of baseball complete, Kiké said he’s been able to explore some new shows, like HBO’s Lanterns and HBO Max’s Peacemaker.

He’s also been thinking about the future as he finds himself listed as a free agent. While the utility player has expressed interest in staying with the Dodgers, he’s found himself thinking more and more about his family as he waits to see what team he may land with next.

“It’s starting to become really hard because my daughter is five and she’s about to start kindergarten. In season, home is Arizona, so for the first semester of kindergarten, we did homeschooling, and now she’s going to enter the school next Monday,” he shared with Us. “Decisions are starting to get really hard because you don’t want to take your kid out of school. I have a second kid now. We have dogs, so the traveling can be a lot.”

As he calls Arizona home, Kiké acknowledged that half of MLB’s teams do spring training in his state while the other half head to Florida.

“It could get hard having to leave your house, leave the family behind to do spring training and be two months by yourself over there, and then have to take your family somewhere else,” he said. “Those are all things that get really hard, and things that people don’t really think about as often as they should from an outside perspective, but life gets very real when it comes to baseball season. Luckily, we’re fortunate enough to have a good support system and to make the transition easier.”

It's the start of a new month, which means new additions and departures on Xbox Game Pass. Simulator fans can say goodbye to Football Manager 26, Firefighting Simulator, Pigeon Simulator, and Police Simulator this month. Believe it or not, those games all come from different developers, as it feels like there's a simulator for every category and hobby out there. Another noteworthy departure is Dragon Ball Xenoverse 2, the action-RPG that was recently upgraded for current-gen consoles. The game has been around for several years and has grown with updates that add new characters and adventures, but with Dragon Ball Xenoverse 3 launching in the second half of 2027, it might be time to wave goodbye to the Time Patrol.

Also on the way are the first Moonlighter, the adorably cozy Winter Burrow, and Barbie Horse Trails. As a reminder, you can save 20% on these games if you decide to buy them before they leave Game Pass.

Leaving Xbox Game Pass on November 15
